Touch the palm side of the R hand down onto the flat palm.
Lift the R hand off an inch or two, shift it downward a couple of inches, and touch down again.
Make the two contacts firm and crisp — the double tap reads as an official rule.
Keep both hands in your chest-level signing space with a matter-of-fact expression.
tip: RULE is LAW initialized: tap an R hand twice on a flat palm.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you with the palm facing up.
Point your dominant index finger straight down toward that open palm.
Jab the fingertip down onto the palm twice in quick, firm taps.
Keep the jabs short and pointed, like marking an amount due on a bill.
Use a single jab for the verb 'owe' and the double jab for the noun 'bill'.
Keep a neutral expression; the taps carry the meaning, not the face.
tip: Double-jab your open palm with an index finger — like pointing out the total on an invoice.

steps: Raise both hands in front of you in V handshapes, index and middle fingers extended.
Hold your non-dominant V hand steady with the fingers pointing up and the palm facing back.
Rest the fingertips of your dominant V lightly on top of the non-dominant fingertips.
Flutter the dominant index and middle fingers up and down in alternation, like a see-saw.
Keep the base hand still while only the top fingers rock back and forth.
Pair it with raised eyebrows when you ask a choice question, such as TEA EITHER COFFEE?
tip: Two V hands rocking fingertip to fingertip — picture weighing two choices against each other.

steps: Hold up your non-dominant hand in a five handshape, palm facing toward your dominant side and fingers pointing up.
Flatten your dominant hand into a B shape, fingers together and thumb tucked in.
Slide the pinkie-side edge of the flat hand down between the middle and ring fingers of the raised hand.
Move it as if slipping a document into a file folder.
Do the insertion once for the verb 'to file', twice for the noun 'a file or document'.
Keep the raised hand steady and upright while the flat hand does the work.
tip: Slipping the flat hand between the upright fingers is filing a document into a folder — twice for the noun.

steps: Raise both hands up high near head height, off to your dominant side.
Start with the hands in the loose open shape used for QUOTE or TITLE.
Sweep both hands downward toward the front of your torso.
As the hands drop, bend the index and middle fingers into bent-V shapes.
Land the movement in front of your chest or stomach, showing data coming down to you.
Keep the path smooth and vertical — the downward travel is what says 'download'.
tip: Hands start high and rain down into bent Vs at your torso — files coming down to your device.

steps: Hold both hands up in front of your chest in open five handshapes, fingers spread.
Start with the palms facing you and the fingertips pointing upward.
Twist both wrists sharply so the palms snap to face outward, away from you.
Make the twist quick and decisive — one firm twist says the matter is FINAL.
Keep the elbows relaxed and the hands close together in your central signing space.
Match a firm, settled expression to the finality of the statement.
tip: One sharp twist of both open hands from palm-in to palm-out — a single twist reads as 'final'.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand out in front of you as a flat hand, fingers together, palm facing down.
Shape your dominant hand into a flat hand too, with the fingers slightly bent and relaxed.
Bring the pinky edge of your dominant hand down onto the back of your non-dominant hand.
Brush your dominant hand across the back of the other hand in one short swipe, ending just past its edge.
Keep the wrist loose so the brush-off motion stays quick, light, and easy.
Keep a neutral or pleasant face, since this sign is about a low price, not something bad.
tip: One quick brush-off across a flat hand — picture wiping a price tag down to something small.

steps: Raise your dominant index finger to your lips, touching the fingertip to them lightly.
Point the finger slightly sideways so your palm faces your non-dominant side.
Push your hand forward several inches in one quick, firm motion.
Keep the finger stiff and the movement short, stopping cleanly at the end.
Pair the sign with a confident nod and steady eye contact when you want to affirm something.
tip: One production does heavy duty: it also covers sure, indeed, really, very, and you're welcome in context.

steps: Touch the fingertips of your dominant flat hand to your lips or chin, palm facing you.
Move your hand down and away from your face in one smooth arc.
As your hand travels, twist it so your palm rotates to face downward.
End with your hand open in front of your chest, palm facing down.
Wear a frown or scowl to match the meaning — the face carries the negativity.
tip: BAD is the mirror image of GOOD: same start at the mouth, but the palm twists down instead of up.

steps: Form both hands into A fists, with your thumbs tucked up along the fingers.
Press the two fists together in front of your chest, palms facing each other.
Keeping the fists touching, stir them in a flat horizontal circle, as if mixing a pot.
Make one full, smooth sweep of the circle in a single continuous movement.
Hold your torso relaxed and keep your eyes on your conversation partner.
tip: Start from the WITH sign — two fists pressed together — then stir. The circling motion is what says 'all of us as one.'

steps: Hold your dominant hand up beside your cheek as a fist, with the thumb sticking up like the letter A.
Keep the fist steady and flick the thumb upward in one quick, single motion.
Let the thumb pop up and freeze for a beat before relaxing the hand.
Make the motion short and decisive — one flick, not a repeated wiggle.
Keep a neutral, questioning face when you use it in a sentence like 'who else?'
tip: Lifeprint teaches OTHER and ELSE as the same sign: one quick thumb-flick up. Do it twice and you are signing TEN instead.

steps: Hold both hands out in front of your torso as flat hands, palms facing down.
Keep your fingers together and the hands roughly shoulder-width apart.
Move both hands straight downward a few inches in one smooth, even motion.
Keep the hands level with each other through the whole drop.
Hold a neutral, matter-of-fact expression, since this is a plain noun sign.
tip: This is Lifeprint's non-initialized PERSON sign — no P handshapes needed — and it doubles as the AGENT suffix in signs like TEACH-PERSON.

steps: Hold your dominant hand out in front of you, palm facing down, at about chest height.
Pat the air once downward, as if patting the head of a small child standing in front of you.
Shift your hand a few inches to the side and pat the air a second time.
Make each pat a single short, light dip of the hand.
Keep a warm, friendly face, since the sign conjures two little kids in front of you.
tip: Lifeprint's trick: one quick pat per child, two imaginary heads — that is what turns CHILD into KIDS without any extra sign.

steps: Close both hands into S fists, with your thumbs folded across your fingers.
Hold the fists in front of your chest with the thumb sides facing each other and the palms facing down.
Strike the knuckle sides of your fists together.
Hit them together a second time, as if knocking two stones against each other.
Keep the strikes crisp and close to your chest, letting the soundless knock carry the meaning.
tip: Knuckles-to-knuckles twice — the collision of the two S fists is what makes the stone 'hard.'

steps: Shape both hands into L handshapes, with your thumbs resting between your index and middle fingers.
Wrap each index finger around the outside edge of its thumb, keeping both hands in front of your chest.
Snap both thumbs upward and back in one quick motion, landing in modified X handshapes.
Make the snap small and sharp, ending with the thumbs raised slightly rather than wide.
Keep your palms facing each other through the motion and your elbows relaxed at your sides.
Pair the sign with an energetic expression, making it bigger and sharper to mean even faster.
tip: Think of flicking something off your fingertips — that snap of the thumbs is the whole sign.

steps: Extend both index fingers upright, keeping your other fingers and thumbs tucked closed.
Hold the hands out in front of your chest about a foot apart, with your palms facing each other.
Bring the two hands toward each other until their lower edges meet in the middle.
Do not let the fingertips touch — the meeting happens at the base of the hands.
Aim the movement between the two people or spots to show who is meeting whom.
Keep your eyes on the meeting point and give a slight nod for a friendly greeting.
tip: Two index fingers walk toward each other like two people; for a whole group, switch to the MEETING sign.

steps: Form both hands into modified A handshapes, with your thumbs tucked up alongside your index fingers.
Hold your non-dominant A hand still in front of you as a fixed starting point.
Start with your dominant A hand touching or close to the non-dominant hand.
Move the dominant hand outward and away from the base hand in one firm, single motion.
Travel the full length of your arm to show real distance, ending with the arm extended.
Point your eyes and face toward the direction of travel to mark far away.
tip: Your non-dominant hand is home base — the dominant hand walks away from it. An index-finger version can point at a real far-off place.

steps: Form your dominant hand into an open X, with your thumb extended upward off the fist.
Raise the hand to about chin or forehead height in front of your body.
Pull the hand straight downward in one smooth motion toward your chest.
As the hand drops, fold the thumb down so it lands against your index finger's middle knuckle.
Finish with a closed X handshape, the thumb's knuckle tucked against the index finger.
Use a single downward pull for the verb; a double pull makes the noun SUBSCRIPTION.
tip: Picture reaching up and yanking a fresh magazine or paycheck down out of the air — the sign means receiving something regularly.

steps: Open your dominant hand into a five handshape with all fingers spread wide.
Bend only the middle finger forward at its large knuckle, leaving the other fingers straight and open.
Place the fingertip of the bent middle finger against your chest, directly over your heart.
Poke your chest twice with that fingertip in a quick, light double tap.
Hold the rest of the hand open and relaxed while the middle finger does the tapping.
Stay neutral-faced; the double poke at the heart carries the meaning of the sign.
tip: The bent middle finger points at the heart like an arrow — one poke instead of two would mean 'touched,' not 'heart.'

steps: Raise both hands in front of you with only the index fingers extended upward.
Close the remaining fingers on each hand so just the index fingers stand out.
Flutter both index fingers up and down in a quick, small wiggling motion.
As the fingers flutter, move both hands apart, out to the sides.
Keep the motion small and quick — the fingers flutter, not the whole arms.
Stay neutral-faced; the fluttering index fingers carry the meaning of the sign.
tip: Think of your fingertips fluttering over many different choices at once. Do not confuse it with VARYING, which is a much larger wrist-and-elbow motion.

steps: Make an H handshape with each hand, extending the index and middle fingers together.
Hold your non-dominant H hand flat and steady in front of your chest.
Set the dominant H hand on top of the non-dominant hand.
Rock the dominant hand back and forth in a quick double movement, like a balancing scale.
Keep the non-dominant hand completely still while the dominant hand does the rocking.
Stay neutral-faced; the rocking scale motion carries the meaning.
tip: One sign covers POUND, WEIGHT, and WEIGH — picture the two H hands like an old balance scale weighing something out.

steps: Hold both hands flat with the fingers held together in front of your chest.
Touch the fingertips of both hands together, forming the peaked shape of a rooftop.
Move both hands a little to the side while separating them slightly.
Touch the fingertips together again in the new position, forming a second rooftop.
Keep your palms angled down and toward each other so each rooftop keeps its peak.
Stay neutral-faced; the pair of rooftops stands for a town's buildings.
tip: This is the same sign as CITY — the double rooftop is the town's skyline.

steps: Bend both hands at the knuckles, keeping the fingers curved and relaxed.
Hold your non-dominant bent hand low in front of you as the base.
Lay your dominant bent hand directly on top of the base hand.
Alternate the hands, stacking each new layer on top of the last one.
Move the stack upward with every layer, as if building a wall higher.
Keep a neutral face; the upward stacking shows construction in progress.
tip: Think of laying bricks — each alternate layer stacks higher.

steps: Make a Y handshape with each hand, extending the thumb and pinkie.
Hold both Y hands in front of you with the palms facing upward.
Move both hands down a few inches in one firm, sharp drop.
Keep the movement short and crisp rather than a long fall.
Stay neutral-faced; the single drop means 'now,' not a question.
tip: One drop means NOW; repeat the drop and it becomes TODAY — do not double the motion if you mean 'currently.'

steps: Curve both hands in front of your chest so the fingertips of each hand nearly touch, like you are holding a small ball.
Keep the hands centered at chest height, with your palms facing downward toward the floor.
Open both hands outward and apart in one smooth motion until your arms are spread wide, as if clearing a foggy window.
Finish with both hands fully open and flat, palms facing forward and fingers spread wide.
Pair the sign with a calm, certain expression — with the right face it can also mean bright or obvious.
tip: The hands wipe open as if clearing away blur; with a knowing nod it reads as 'obvious.'

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a C, curving your thumb and fingertips toward each other.
Hold the C-hand in front of your torso at the midline, beside your non-dominant hand, which stays still as a marker.
Slide the dominant hand sideways toward your dominant side in a short, firm path, like marking off a section.
Let the C-handshape open and flatten as it travels, finishing as a flat hand, palm facing down.
Keep your face neutral and relaxed — this is a straightforward content sign with no special grammar marker.
tip: An initialized sign: the C-handshape stands for the letter C in 'chapter.'

steps: Form both hands into hooked index-finger handshapes and stack them, with your dominant hand resting on top of the other.
Start the stacked hands off to one side of your signing space, near the person doing the lending.
Move the stacked hands in one straight path toward the borrower, as if passing an invisible object.
Keep the palms of the stacked hands facing down as they travel the full path.
Finish with the hands near the borrower — point the movement toward whoever receives the money or object.
tip: The same sign works for LEND and BORROW; flip the movement direction to flip who gives and who receives.

steps: Close both hands into fists, as if gripping a pair of horse reins.
Hold the fists in front of your chest about a foot apart, at the same height, palms facing inward.
Slide the hands alternately forward and back, like pulling reins to steer a horse.
Then add the agent marker: bring both flat hands to your sides with palms facing each other.
Glide the flat hands straight down past your torso to mean 'person,' completing the compound sign.
tip: Two-part sign: the reins-pulling CONTROL plus the 'person' marker — together they mean 'one who manages.'

steps: Extend the index finger of your dominant hand upward, keeping your other fingers and thumb closed.
Hold the hand out in front of you at a comfortable angle, tilted slightly back rather than straight up.
Turn your palm so it faces back toward you through the whole sign.
Drop your hand down a few inches while quickly opening your middle finger beside the index finger, changing the 1 into a 2.
End with the two fingers side by side at the lower position, keeping the motion short and crisp.
tip: The quick 1-to-2 switch shows the 'half' being counted off — keep the drop small, not a big swing.

steps: Hold both hands out in front of your torso as flat hands, palms facing down, as if each hand were a foot.
Keep your non-dominant hand still and low in front of you, acting as the back foot.
Lift your dominant hand up a few inches, letting the fingers tilt upward like a foot lifting off the ground.
Swing the raised hand forward past the stationary hand, moving in a short stepping arc.
Set the dominant hand down in its new forward position, finishing with both hands flat and palms down.
tip: Your hands mime feet — the lift-and-place of the stepping hand is what names this sign.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a C, with the thumb and fingers curved toward each other.
Close your non-dominant hand into a fist, with the thumb resting along the front of the fingers.
Rest the thumb of your C hand on the back of the fist, just behind the knuckles.
Tap the thumb up and down against the back of the fist, once or twice, in a straight vertical motion.
Keep the movement up and down only — never circle the thumb around.
Hold the fist steady in front of your chest and keep your face calm and neutral while signing.
tip: Think of the ROCK sign with a C hand — the thumb taps the rock to build the church.

steps: Curl both hands into O shapes, with each thumb touching the fingertips.
Hold the O hands out in front of you, below chest height, with the palms facing each other and angled slightly forward.
Push both hands forward in one quick motion, letting them drift slightly outward as they go.
Shake your head once to the side as the hands move forward.
Sign it lower and quicker than TEACH — the whole motion is small and direct.
tip: Unlike TEACH, the hands angle outward and sit low — one headshake seals the meaning.

steps: Make an A handshape with your dominant hand — a fist with the thumb resting up along the side.
Extend the index finger of your non-dominant hand and hold it out in front of you.
Brush the side of your dominant fist upward against the top edge of that index finger.
Repeat the brushing motion once or twice, keeping it small and controlled.
Keep the non-dominant index finger planted and steady while the fist brushes past it.
tip: Picture polishing a shoe — you are polishing up your skills.

steps: Hold both hands in front of your chest in loose, relaxed 5-handshapes with your fingers slightly bent.
Angle both hands forward and slightly downward, with the fingertips pointing out and down.
Pump both hands forward and down, then back up, in a small repeated bouncing motion.
Keep your palms angled forward and down for the whole movement.
Use a relaxed, casual mouth shape, since chatting is informal, easy conversation.
tip: One-handed and two-handed loose-C versions also exist, but the two-handed 5-hand bounce is the most common.

steps: Make a fist with your non-dominant hand and hold it out in front of your torso, knuckles up.
Open your dominant hand flat with the fingers held together, palm facing down.
Sweep the flat hand forward across the top of the fist in one smooth, firm pass away from your body.
tip: ENOUGH mirrors FULL: FULL glides the flat hand backward over the fist, while ENOUGH glides it forward.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand open and flat in front of you, palm facing up like a page of paper.
Touch the tip of your dominant index finger to the dip of your dominant thumb, as if holding a pen.
Scribble quickly across the open palm with small side-to-side strokes, as if writing a note.
Keep your dominant palm facing down or slightly toward you while you scribble.
Hold the non-dominant hand steady; it does not move while the other hand writes.
tip: For 'wrote a paper' use one quick downward stroke; for 'write your name' use one careful sideways stroke.

steps: Extend both index fingers and hold your hands out in front of your torso, fingers pointing straight forward.
Curl the other fingers down into your palms and angle your palms slightly downward.
Flick both index fingers upward in one quick, sharp snapping motion.
Keep the movement brisk and short, ending with the fingertips pointing up.
tip: A related snap with the thumbs tucked between the fingers means 'fast' or 'immediately' instead.

steps: Open your dominant hand into a 5-handshape with all fingers spread.
Hold the hand beside your face at cheek height, palm facing back toward your own face.
Draw one full circle around your face in the air, keeping the hand open the whole time.
Keep the palm facing back toward you as it circles.
tip: The 5-hand version means looks or appearance; tracing the circle with just an index finger simply means a face.

steps: Fingerspell O-I-L with your dominant hand, holding it at shoulder height.
Flow the three letters together smoothly and quickly, without pausing between them.
Keep your palm angled forward toward your conversation partner as you spell.
Keep the movement compact and relaxed, the way Deaf signers blend common fingerspelled words.
tip: OIL is a lexicalized fingerspelling: Deaf signers spell it fast as one blended unit rather than three separate letters.

steps: Bring your dominant thumb and fingertips together so they nearly touch, leaving only a tiny gap.
Hold the pinched hand up in front of your chest at a comfortable height.
Angle your palm inward toward yourself and give the pinch a tiny wiggle to show the small amount.
tip: The smaller the gap between thumb and fingertips, the smaller the amount you are describing.

steps: Form both hands into H-handshapes, index and middle fingers extended together and pointing sideways.
Hold both hands close together in the signing space in front of your chest.
Turn your non-dominant palm down and your dominant palm up to start.
Move the dominant hand up and then down onto the non-dominant fingers, ending with the dominant palm facing down.
tip: Puff your cheeks slightly while signing INCREASE to mean gaining weight; keep a neutral face for a raise or a rising price.

steps: Close both hands into fists and bring them together in front of your chest, one stacked on the other.
Place the dominant fist on top of the non-dominant fist so the knuckles touch.
Twist both wrists together at the same time, as if screwing two pieces into place.
Keep both palms facing inward toward each other through the twist.
Use a focused, deliberate expression, as if building or forming something.
tip: ASL shows past time with a time sign like BEFORE or PAST, so 'created' is this same MAKE movement plus the time marker.

steps: Form a K-handshape with your dominant hand: index finger pointing straight up, middle finger bent down.
Hold the hand beside your forehead, with the middle-finger tip close to your temple.
Trace a small circle in the air beside your temple.
Finish the circle by touching the tip of your middle finger to your forehead.
tip: POLITICAL is GOVERNMENT initialized with a P/K handshape: same temple circle, different fingers.

steps: Form a Y-handshape with your dominant hand by stretching your thumb and pinkie wide while folding the middle fingers down.
Raise the hand to chest height in front of you with the palm facing down.
Press the hand firmly downward in one short, decisive stroke, as if pinning something in place.
Hold the Y-handshape rigid the whole time, keeping the thumb and pinkie fully extended.
Repeat the downward press with both hands together when you want extra emphasis.
Keep a firm, settled expression — this is a command to hold position, not a question.
tip: Lifeprint notes STAY can be signed with one hand or both — either version is understood.

steps: Form a K-handshape with your dominant hand: point your index and middle fingers upward with the thumb tucked between them.
Set the K-hand just below your non-dominant shoulder at the top of your chest.
Sweep the hand diagonally across your torso in one straight stroke, ending near your opposite hip.
Keep the palm angled inward toward your body for the entire sweep.
Move smoothly and evenly — imagine tracing the sash a monarch wears across the chest.
Hold a neutral, dignified expression; a slight chin lift suits the royal meaning.
tip: The diagonal path copies a royal sash — the 1910 manual and modern dictionaries agree on this stroke.

steps: Hold both hands out in front of your torso at waist height with your palms facing down.
Keep your fingers relaxed and loosely open; do not curl or flex them at any point.
Churn both hands in an alternating circular motion, as if kneading a lump of dough.
Drive the movement from your shoulders and elbows, never from your wrists or fingers.
Continue the churning for a second or two with a steady, easy rhythm.
Keep a neutral, matter-of-fact expression — this is the general sign for being busy doing things.
tip: Same sign as ACTIVE and DO — it covers general activity, actions, and 'doing stuff' alike.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing up, like a blank sheet of paper.
Reach your dominant open hand out over the flat hand with all five fingers spread.
Pinch the fingertips and thumb of the dominant hand together, as if lifting an invisible print off the page.
Pull the pinched hand back toward yourself in one smooth, short motion.
Set the pinched fingertips down onto the flat palm of your non-dominant hand.
Keep your expression neutral; the pinch-and-lift motion is what makes the sign readable.
tip: Mime pulling a fresh copy off the original — the pinch-and-lift is the heart of this sign.

steps: Curl your dominant hand into a flattened O, thumb and fingertips nearly touching.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of your torso as a landing pad.
Tap the flattened O hand down onto the flat palm once or twice.
Keep the tapping hand's palm facing down and the base palm facing up.
Keep a neutral face; the quick tap carries the whole meaning.
tip: The same sign as MONEY — context tells listeners you mean cash specifically.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, fingers together, like a tray.
Position it at chest height so the flat palm is a clear landing surface.
Shape your dominant hand into a C above the far edge of that palm.
Pull the C hand back toward yourself along the length of the flat palm.
Close the C into a loose S fist while it travels, as if grabbing coins.
Keep the base hand's palm facing up and your face neutral throughout.
tip: Sign it like EARN — a grab that brings pay toward your body.

steps: Close your non-dominant hand into an S fist and hold it at chest height.
Lay your dominant hand flat on top of that fist, fingers together.
Move the flat hand in a smooth circle on top of the fist.
Keep the flat hand's palm facing down while it circles.
Keep a neutral face; the circle outlines the region's boundary.
tip: Same sign as REGION — the circle traces the edge of an area.

steps: Sign SEE first: shape your dominant hand into a V, index and middle fingers extended.
Hold the V just below your eyes with the fingertips pointing forward.
Move the V hand straight outward away from your face.
Keep the V's palm facing inward toward your face during the move.
Then sign FINISH: brush your dominant flat hand downward across the other flat hand.
Keep a neutral face; FINISH marks the seeing as completed, like have seen.
tip: SEE plus FINISH — the added FINISH turns see into the perfect tense, have seen.

steps: Sign START: hold your non-dominant hand flat and upright in front of you.
Hook your dominant index finger against the edge of that flat hand.
Twist your dominant wrist in a small turn, as if turning a key.
Then sign PAST: raise your dominant flat hand beside your head.
Move the flat hand inward until it nearly touches your shoulder.
Keep the hand's palm facing your shoulder and your face neutral.
tip: Sign START, then the PAST marker — ASL marks past time with time signs, not word endings.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a G, thumb pinched against the bent index finger.
Hold the G hand beside your temple, a few inches out from your head.
Draw one small circle in the air next to your temple.
Finish by touching the fingertips lightly against your temple.
Angle the G so the fingertips point toward your head with a calm, neutral face.
tip: Use the same sign as GOVERNMENT — it covers both the institution and the administration in power.

steps: Curl both index fingers into hooked X shapes, as if each hand is pinching a tiny slip of paper.
Hold both hooked hands in front of your chest, about a foot apart.
Circle the two hands around each other once, trading places in the air.
End with both hands back where they started, the X hooks facing each other.
Keep a neutral face — the circling shows a straight swap with no tricks.
tip: The hands trade places in the air but land where they began, like swapping two items and staying put.

steps: Press your thumbs together with the other fingers tucked into loose fists.
Hold the joined hands a few inches in front of your chest or upper belly.
Push both hands smoothly forward about six inches, away from your body.
Keep both palms angled downward for the whole forward glide.
Hold a steady, determined face — the motion says the action keeps going.
tip: Push forward hard and stop dead, and CONTINUE becomes PERMANENT.

steps: Close your dominant hand into an S fist, thumb resting across the fingers.
Hold your non-dominant hand open and flat in front of you, palm facing up.
Circle the S fist once just above the open palm.
Land the side of the S fist down onto the open palm.
Keep the circle small and smooth, like one turn of the year.
tip: An S circling down onto the palm pictures the cycle of the four seasons; many signers fingerspell SEASON for TV or sports seasons.

steps: Extend your dominant index finger, keeping the other fingers curled into your palm.
Hold your arm out in front of you with the palm facing up.
Draw a small circle, about the size of a quarter, with your index fingertip.
Drive the circle from your arm, keeping the wrist steady and relaxed.
Keep your face neutral — the sign names a plain, unspecified person.
tip: The same sign also means something, single, alone, or only — context picks the meaning.

steps: Point your non-dominant index finger straight up in front of your chest, like a small post.
Shape your dominant hand into a V, index and middle fingers extended and spread.
Bring the V hand down over the upright finger so the finger rests between the two prongs.
Aim the V fingertips downward as the hand settles onto the finger.
Keep a businesslike, neutral expression — this is the paperwork version of apply.
tip: A second popular version looks like VOLUNTEER and means apply for or run for office; the V-over-1 version covers apply to, application, and file.

steps: Open your dominant hand flat, fingers together and extended.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing down.
Slide the flat dominant hand across the back of the non-dominant hand, from one side to the other.
Keep the dominant palm facing down as it glides over the back of the other hand.
Make the pass in one clean stroke — the crossing path is the whole meaning.
tip: This is the same sign as OVER — it also covers across and after in time.

steps: Pinch your dominant thumb and index finger together into a small pincer, like holding a stamp.
Raise your non-dominant index finger upright in front of your chest, palm angled sideways.
Tap the pinching hand once against the side of the upright finger.
Angle the pinching hand's palm toward the finger as it taps.
Keep your face neutral — one tap names the machine that prints.
tip: Same sign as PRINT — context decides whether you mean the action or the machine; a person who prints is PRINT plus PERSON.

steps: Close your dominant hand into an A fist, thumb pressed along the side of the fingers.
Hold the fist in front of your chest with the palm facing left and the thumb-side up.
Twist your wrist so the hand finishes palm down, thumb-side still facing left.
Make the twist one smooth turn, like sweeping through every option.
Pair it with a casual, open face — anything goes.
tip: The ANY sign doubles as ANYTHING; adding the separate THING sign after it is optional, not required.

steps: Bring both hands together in front of your chest with the fingertips touching.
Turn both hands so the palms face down while your fingers relax and loosen.
Drop your hands a few inches, as if something slipped out from between them.
Finish with open, relaxed hands and a neutral, matter-of-fact expression.
tip: Use this only for misplaced things, like lost keys — losing a game or competition is a different sign.

steps: Form both hands into O shapes, with each thumb touching its fingertips.
Hold the O hands out in front of you, palms facing each other and slightly forward.
Push both hands forward a few inches in one quick, smooth motion.
Shake your head no once as your hands move forward.
tip: You can sign this one-handed, but never drop the single headshake — it carries the whole meaning.

steps: Open your dominant hand into a loose five shape with the fingers spread.
Touch your chin with the thumb of that open hand.
Sweep the hand forward and slightly sideways in one or two small arches.
Angle your palm inward toward your face as the hand travels.
Lower your eyebrows a little, as if asking which option is preferred.
tip: Lifeprint glosses this sign PREFER — signing YOU PREFER PIZZA OR HAMBURGER? is how you ask 'Would you rather have pizza or a hamburger?'; some signers close the hand into an A as it moves.

steps: Curl your thumb down onto your palm while extending your pinky finger upward, folding your middle three fingers down too.
Hold the hand up in front of your shoulder, in the signing space at about chin height.
Keep the handshape perfectly still and steady — the number six has no movement of its own.
Face the back of your hand outward toward the person you are signing to, away from yourself.
Keep a neutral, matter-of-fact expression when signing a number in isolation.
tip: Numbers 6–9 are palm-out while 1–5 are palm-in when signed alone — mixing them up is the classic beginner mistake.

steps: Open your dominant hand into a flat five handshape, spreading all five fingers wide.
Touch the tip of your thumb to the center of your chest, just below your collarbone.
Slide the hand a few inches outward and away from your chest, leading with the thumb.
Keep the palm angled slightly toward yourself as the hand glides forward off the chest.
Smile softly or keep a relaxed face — this sign means being okay, not making a payment.
tip: Never use this for fee, cost, thin, or small — Lifeprint warns the sign only covers feeling okay or something being cool.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand out in front of you, flat and open with the palm facing down.
Rest the fingertips of your dominant hand on the back of that hand, starting in a flat O handshape.
Slide the dominant hand outward across the back of the base hand while opening it into a spread five handshape.
Repeat the short outward slide a second time — the noun form uses two quick movements.
Keep both palms facing down the whole time, as if laying opinions out on a table for someone.
tip: The verb advise uses one long movement; the noun advice repeats it twice, short and quick.

steps: Curl both hands into tight A fists, pressing each thumb firmly against the folded index finger.
Raise your right A fist to your chest and your left A fist to the left side of your abdomen.
Start with both fists hovering about two inches out from your body.
Thump both fists inward against your body twice in a quick in-out-in double motion.
Keep both palms facing toward your body for the entire movement, like gripping a rifle.
Hold a straight, upright posture with a serious, matter-of-fact expression.
tip: Picture both fists gripping a rifle held across the chest — the mime is the memory hook for this sign.

steps: Open both hands into relaxed five handshapes, spreading your fingers wide apart.
Hold both hands about an inch in front of your upper chest, thumbs closest to your body.
Brush both hands straight down your chest as if smoothing a shirt, letting the thumbs drag lightly.
Repeat the downward brush a second time in a quick double movement.
Angle your palms slightly toward yourself so the thumbs stay near your chest as they slide.
Keep a neutral expression — actual chest contact is optional; the double brush is what counts.
tip: One large single brush downward means DRESS or GOWN, not clothes — the double movement is the tell.

steps: Bend your dominant index finger into an X handshape: a loose fist with the index finger hooked.
Hold the X hand out in front of you, slightly to the right of center.
Snap the hand downward from the wrist in one firm stroke, ending with the palm facing down.
Start the stroke with the palm facing forward, then let it rotate to palm-down as you bend.
Use a strong, urgent facial expression — the harder and faster the stroke, the more mandatory it feels.
tip: This is the same production Lifeprint glosses as need, must, and have-to — keep it forceful to carry the 'no choice' sense.

steps: Touch the tip of your dominant index finger to your right temple to begin.
Slide your dominant hand downward while changing the index finger into an "F" handshape.
Raise your non-dominant hand into a matching "F" handshape beside the moving hand.
When both hands reach lower-chest level, drop them sharply downward a few inches and stop dead.
tip: A shorter version starts directly in F hands and drops once — it also means "determine".

steps: Shape both hands into hooked claws: curl your index fingers like hooks and keep your thumbs extended outward.
Hold both hands in front of your chest with the palms facing each other and the fingertips close together.
Pull your hands apart in a wide, forceful motion, spreading your arms broadly to show great size.
Open your mouth into a "cha" shape and widen your eyes to intensify the meaning.
tip: "Huge" is the BIG/LARGE sign made bigger and bolder — the "cha" mouth shape turns "big" into "huge".

steps: Bend the middle finger of your dominant hand at the large knuckle so its tip points downward.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you with its palm facing up.
Circle the bent middle-finger tip above the upturned palm, then plant the fingertip into its center.
Hold the planted fingertip still for a moment to mark the exact middle point.
tip: Use the bent finger for "middle" — a flat circling hand instead means "center".

steps: Bend both wrists so your open hands point downward, with the fingertips aiming at the floor.
Hold both hands in front of your body at waist height with the palms facing back toward you.
Pivot both hands toward and away from your body in one quick motion to sign SELL.
Raise both flat hands to chest height with the palms facing each other, then move them straight downward.
Keep the flat hands level with each other as they drop, forming the PERSON agent suffix.
tip: SELL plus the flat-hand PERSON sign means "a person who sells"; ASL shows plural through context, not a new sign.

steps: Extend your dominant hand forward with the fingers together and the palm angled upward.
Curl your fingers inward as if grabbing an invisible object out of the air.
Pull your closed hand back toward your chest in one smooth, decisive motion.
Turn your palm to face your body as the hand arrives near your chest.
tip: TAKE-from pulls toward you to mean "get from someone"; TAKE-up lifts high to mean "take a class" or "adopt".

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand steady in front of you at about waist height.
Bring your dominant hand down an inch or two until it makes contact with the other hand.
Move both hands together downward and outward to the sides in one smooth motion.
End with the hands separated, picturing a whole quantity splitting into parts.
tip: This general DIVIDE sign works for math and for "split" — a fancy initialized math version exists but is not needed.

steps: Point both index fingers forward so the two fingertips aim toward each other.
Rotate the two index fingers around one another in a small circular motion.
Draw both hands toward your body in one smooth arcing movement.
Keep your palms angled inward toward yourself as the hands arrive near your chest.
tip: The same circling motion moves away from you to mean "go" — direction decides coming versus going.

steps: Form an "L" handshape with your dominant hand, extending your thumb and index finger.
Place the "L" handshape against your chin with the index finger touching the chin.
Bounce the hand gently on your chin two times while keeping the "L" handshape firm.
Keep your palm angled inward toward your face throughout the two bounces.
tip: The modern preference is the chin — an older version touched the upper lip instead.

steps: Close both hands into fists and hold them in front of your chest.
Angle the fists toward each other so the knuckles face inward like meshing gears.
Interlock the fingers loosely, then move the hands back and forth in small alternating twists.
Keep the movement compact and rhythmic, as if you are turning a set of gears.
tip: One sign covers machine, motor, engine, and factory — context tells you which meaning applies.

steps: Curl both hands into loose fists with each thumb sticking straight up, like signing the number ten.
Hold your non-dominant fist out in front of your chest, thumb up, as the person being followed.
Set your dominant fist a few inches directly behind the non-dominant one, also thumb up.
Move both fists forward together a short distance, keeping the dominant hand trailing behind the other.
Keep both palms facing sideways and your thumbs upright for the whole forward motion.
Look steadily forward as the hands move, as if watching the person ahead of you.
tip: The following hand always trails — if the dominant hand drifts ahead, you are signing 'chase', not 'follow'.

steps: Raise your non-dominant forearm upright in front of your chest, elbow low, like a tree trunk.
Curve your dominant hand into a C, with the thumb and fingers forming a firm half circle.
Rest the wrist of the C hand on top of the upright forearm.
Rock the C hand left and right twice from the wrist, with the same sway as the sign for TREE.
Keep the trunk arm perfectly still so that only the C hand does the moving.
tip: The C is an initialization of the sign TREE — do not sign TREE separately; CHRISTMAS + TREE together means 'Christmas tree'.

steps: Press your dominant thumb against your index fingertip to form a small pinching shape.
Hold the pinched fingers out in front of your chest, facing an imaginary row of options.
Close the fingers onto one option and lift the hand upward and toward your chest.
Angle your palm downward while you draw the selected option inward.
Finish with a small decisive nod of the head, since choosing is an intentional and confident act.
tip: The same citation sign as CHOOSE — the noun 'choice' and the verb 'choose' are signed identically in ASL.

steps: Cross the middle finger of your dominant hand over its index finger to form an R.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing upward like a paper form.
Lay the R hand down across the fingers of the open palm.
Lift the R, shift it a couple of inches toward the wrist, and set it down again.
Make the double stamp motion with a matter-of-fact expression, as if handling paperwork.
tip: The same citation sign as REGISTER — in casual conversation many signers swap this for the small scribbling SIGNATURE sign.

steps: Straighten your dominant index finger while the other fingers curl into the palm.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat, fingers together, in front of your chest.
Touch the tip of the index finger into the V between the other hand's index and middle fingers.
Rotate the index finger once or twice, a short twist as if turning a small key.
Keep the twisting palm facing sideways, with a bright expression that matches a new beginning.
tip: The same citation sign as START — a small repeated twist marks the ongoing 'starting' meaning in ASL.

steps: Open your non-dominant hand into a flat five with the fingers together and pointing forward.
Hold that flat hand out in front of your chest with its palm facing sideways.
Cup your dominant hand around the fingertips of the flat hand, catching them from above.
Pull both hands forward together in one firm motion, the dominant hand drawing the other along.
Keep the base hand steady while your dominant hand does the pulling.
Look engaged and forward-facing, the way a leader watches where the group is going.
tip: One strong pull means 'lead' — double the motion and it reads as 'leadership'.

steps: Make an 'I love you' handshape with your dominant hand, extending your thumb, index finger, and pinkie.
Hold the hand in the space in front of your shoulder at about chest height.
Glide the hand forward twice in short, even movements, as if a plane were cruising onward.
Keep your palm facing the floor through the entire movement.
Look in the direction your hand travels with a relaxed, neutral expression.
tip: This is the same production as AIRPLANE — context tells them apart: DRIVE-to AIRPORT versus GET-in AIRPLANE.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing up, as your canvas.
Make an 'I' handshape with your dominant hand, extending only your pinkie finger.
Touch the pad of your pinkie to the flat palm and draw a few short strokes, as if sketching with a pencil.
Then add the person marker: hold both flat hands out at your sides with fingers pointing outward.
Sweep both flat hands straight down along your torso, keeping the palms facing each other.
Finish the movement with a slight nod, as if presenting the finished artist.
tip: ART is Lifeprint's DRAW sign done with a pinkie brush — adding the flat-hands-down person ending turns an action into its doer, the same pattern as TEACHER.

steps: Make an 'F' handshape with your dominant hand, touching your thumb to your index finger and spreading the other three fingers.
Hold the hand out at chest height with the palm facing forward.
Wave the hand from side to side a couple of times using small, tight movements.
Keep the path strictly side to side and never let the hand circle.
Keep a neutral, matter-of-fact expression while signing.
tip: Side-to-side is FURNITURE; drawing a circle with the same 'F' hand means FRIDAY — the classic beginner mix-up.

steps: Form an 'F' handshape with each hand, touching each thumb to its index finger and spreading the other fingers.
Hold both hands in front of your chest with the palms facing down toward the floor.
Start with the hands close together near the center of your chest.
Move both hands away from each other in opposite directions in one smooth, even motion.
Keep your palms facing down and your elbows relaxed through the whole movement.
Hold a calm, neutral expression as you finish.
tip: Picture unrolling a diploma scroll: the 'F' hands show its width and the outward movement its length. For temperature or extent, Lifeprint points to a different DEGREE sign.

steps: Make an 'F' handshape with your dominant hand, touching your thumb to your index finger and spreading the other fingers.
Touch the 'F' hand against your chest or torso where a shirt button would sit.
Arc the hand downward a few inches along your torso.
Touch your torso again to mark the position of a second button.
Repeat once more to show a third button if you want to show several.
Keep a neutral expression and let the taps mark each button's place.
tip: Two or three taps is plenty — the round 'F' handshape already shows the button's shape, so you never need to tap every button on the shirt.

steps: Raise your dominant hand to your forehead with your thumb and fingertips loosely gathered.
Pinch the thumb and fingertips together as if grasping the brim of an imaginary baseball cap.
Give the imaginary brim a small tug forward and slightly downward.
Keep your palm facing down as you tip the cap.
Finish with a relaxed, neutral expression.
tip: Forehead placement marks the masculine set (boy, dad, brother) — a tipped cap from the era when men wore hats; the feminine set is placed at the chin instead.

steps: Make an 'I' handshape with your dominant hand, forming a fist with only the pinkie extended.
Touch the tip of your pinkie against the middle of your forehead.
Flick the pinkie away from your forehead with a small upward jerk.
Shift your hand slightly to one side and repeat the forehead touch and flick once more.
Keep your palm facing outward as the pinkie pops off the forehead.
Raise your eyebrows slightly, as if a bright thought has just struck.
tip: One flick is IDEA; repeating it with a small sideways shift applies ASL's plural sweep — the same doubling that turns CHILD into CHILDREN.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into an A, with the thumb sticking up alongside the fist.
Bring the hand to the side of your face, placing the thumb near your ear.
Slide the tip of the thumb down along your jawbone until it reaches your chin.
Keep the palm facing inward toward your cheek while the thumb traces the jaw line.
Use a calm, neutral face while signing — the meaning is clear from the location alone.
tip: Born from the string of a bonnet tied under the chin — that is why female signs live near the jaw.

steps: Hold both hands in bent B shapes, with the fingers curved and the thumbs alongside.
Raise both hands to your shoulders, letting the fingertips touch down on them.
Tap your shoulders once or twice with the fingertips, using a firm, short contact.
Keep the palms angled down toward your shoulders as the fingertips make contact.
Hold a steady, serious expression — this sign names a duty, so sign it with weight.
tip: Think of the weight of a duty resting on your shoulders — tap twice for ‘responsibility,’ one long hold for ‘you are responsible.’

steps: Shape both hands into open-A hands, with the thumbs raised and slightly forward.
Hold the hands in front of your chest, with the thumbs pointing toward each other.
Move both hands in a small circular motion, keeping them near each other.
Keep the palms facing each other while the thumbs angle up and down.
Wear a friendly, engaged expression — this sign describes people interacting together.
tip: One sign covers associate, socialize, mingle, and hang out with — the ‘associated’ sense comes from context, not a separate sign.

steps: Hold both hands flat and open, with the fingers extended and together.
Raise both hands to the sides of your head, near your ears or temples.
Move both hands forward together in one short, even motion.
Keep the palms facing each other as the hands travel forward.
Direct your eyes and attention forward, showing concentration on the task.
tip: This is the sign Lifeprint glosses ATTENTION-[focus, concentrate, pay-attention] — it covers all three meanings.

steps: Form a flat hand with your dominant hand, fingers pressed together and the thumb resting along the side.
Bring the hand up to the side of your head, near your cheek or temple.
Rest the side of your head against the hand, tilting slightly as if settling onto a pillow.
Keep the palm facing toward your face with the fingers pointing toward your ear.
Hold the position briefly with a relaxed face, as if you are ready to fall asleep.
tip: Use this sign only for the thing you sleep on — for a truck bed or a flower bed, fingerspell B-E-D.

steps: Raise your dominant hand to about shoulder height to begin signing a number.
Hold up one through five fingers for an isolated number, with your palm facing back toward you.
Roll the wrist as you twist from six through ten, keeping the motion small and even.
Turn your palm forward when the number is part of a series, such as a phone number or address.
For a multi-digit number, show the first digit and then the second in quick succession with the same hand.
Keep a neutral face; emphasis comes from the hand position, not from facial expression.
tip: Isolated numbers go palm-back (the least tiring wrist position); sequences, ages, and times go palm-forward.

steps: Spell T with your dominant hand, the thumb resting against the folded index finger.
Shift into a modified O handshape, using only your thumb, index, and middle fingers in a loose ring.
Slide the hand about two inches to the side while the handshape rounds out.
Finish with the L handshape, index finger pointing up and thumb stretched outward.
Keep your palm angled forward toward your conversation partner through the whole movement.
Mouth the word tool naturally while spelling, instead of naming each letter aloud.
tip: TOOL has no widely accepted sign — Deaf signers fingerspell it, blended into one quick, sign-like unit.

steps: Raise both hands in front of your chest with index fingers extended and the other fingers closed.
Point the two index fingers toward each other in the space before your chest.
Rotate both index fingers around one another in small, even circles.
Move both hands toward your body as the fingers circle, pulling the motion inward.
Keep your palms facing roughly inward, the fingertips gliding past each other without touching.
Tilt your head slightly forward with raised eyebrows, as if inviting the person closer.
tip: COME is uninflected — the same production covers come, comes, and coming; direction shows who is moving.

steps: Extend the middle finger of your dominant hand while the other fingers stay loosely curled.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of your chest, palm facing upward like a tray.
Press the middle fingertip into the center of the palm and rock the hand side to side twice.
Keep your dominant palm angled downward as the middle finger pivots in place.
Use a small, relaxed rocking motion — a stiff, wide sweep reads as a different sign.
tip: Think of the middle finger stirring medicine into your palm like a spoon in a cup.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a Y, extending the thumb and pinky while tucking the middle fingers.
Hold the Y handshape beside your head, with the thumb near your ear and the pinky toward your mouth.
Rock the hand with a small double movement, tilting it slightly forward and back twice.
Keep the thumb and pinky extended throughout — folding them in changes the sign entirely.
Keep your face neutral and conversational; TELEPHONE is a plain noun sign.
tip: The thumb is the old earpiece and the pinky the mouthpiece of a rotary handset — the same sign as PHONE.

steps: Form both hands into R handshapes, crossing each middle finger over its index finger.
Hold both R hands in front of your torso, close together or slightly overlapping at the start.
Sweep both hands outward to the sides at the same time, moving each about five inches from center.
Keep both palms angled slightly inward as the hands separate.
Pair the sweep with a firm, confident nod to mean 'I am ready.'
tip: The outward sweep mirrors an umpire signaling 'safe!' — the R hands part like runners taking their marks.

steps: Make the ASL number 9 handshape with both hands, holding only the thumb and index finger out and apart.
Raise both hands to chest height, keeping them a few inches in front of your torso.
Brush the dominant hand's fingertips straight downward across the non-dominant hand's fingertips in one crisp motion.
Point both palms sideways, facing each other, throughout the brushing motion.
Keep your expression neutral and relaxed — the sign is a plain, matter-of-fact comment.
tip: The same sign also means 'simple' or 'easy'; the surrounding sentence tells the reader which sense you mean.

steps: Curl your dominant hand into an E handshape, fingers bent with the thumb tucked beneath them.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of your torso, palm facing upward like a tray.
Tap the dominant E hand down onto the non-dominant palm two times, with a short bounce between taps.
Keep the dominant palm facing upward as it lands, so the curled fingers do the tapping.
Hold an assertive, serious expression — this sign presents something as a proven fact.
tip: Swap the E handshape for a flat hand and the sign reads as PROOF instead.

steps: Hold your dominant hand open with all five fingers extended and spread slightly.
Bring the tip of the dominant middle finger up to touch the front of your chin.
Give the chin one firm, quick jab with the fingertip; do not rub or brush across the skin.
Angle the palm inward toward your face so the middle finger points straight at the chin.
Raise your eyebrows slightly and smile a little — the pleased expression marks it as a genuine favorite.
tip: Jab, never brush: a rubbing motion changes the sign into TASTE instead.

steps: Spread your dominant hand into an open 5-handshape with all fingers extended.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat and horizontal at chest height, palm turned toward your torso.
Draw the dominant hand downward across the flat hand while wiggling all four fingers like falling drops.
Face both palms toward your own torso as the dominant hand slides down.
Do the downward wiggle once or twice depending on the sentence — twice suggests a continuing flow.
tip: The wiggling fingers picture blood trickling down; keep the wiggle small and quick so it reads as flow.

steps: Shape both hands as flat open hands, fingers together with thumbs alongside.
Hold both hands up in the neutral signing space in front of your shoulders.
Move both hands forward together in one smooth, straight motion.
Keep both palms facing each other, like the two walls of a corridor.
Use one firm forward push and keep your expression neutral throughout.
tip: Think of your two flat hands as the walls of a hallway pushing forward; a blended fingerspelled #HALL loan is also used casually.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing up like a counter.
Bring your dominant flat hand down to land on it, palm facing down.
Flip the dominant hand over so its back lands on the same palm again.
Make both landings firm and quick using a small wrist flip.
Keep your body relaxed; no extra ROOM sign is needed after this sign.
tip: Land palm-down, then back-of-hand. Do not confuse it with COOK, which uses a different flipping motion.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a hooked two, with the index and middle fingers bent like claws.
Start the hand off to one side of your body at about chest height.
Swing the hand across to the other side in a smooth downward arc.
Keep the palm angled down toward the floor through the whole arc.
Finish with one confident sweep; a single trip from side to side.
tip: One clawed-two hand arcing side to side — think of switching trains or moving funds between two accounts.

steps: Make a fist with each hand, wrapping the thumbs firmly over the fingers.
Hold both fists in front of your chest with the forearms roughly parallel.
Pull both fists outward and slightly down in one sharp, firm motion.
Keep the fists clenched through the entire movement; never open them.
Flex your arms and set a determined expression to match the meaning.
tip: Fists stay fists the whole time — if the hands start as loose claws that close into fists, you are signing BRAVE instead.

steps: Hold both hands up in front of you with the fingers loosely together.
Rub each thumb against its fingertips in small circles, as if feeling sand or soil.
Keep both hands working side by side at about chest height.
Angle the palms toward your body while the thumbs keep rubbing.
Use a neutral expression and repeat the rubbing two or three times.
tip: This is the DIRT sign — it also covers soil, sand, land, and the ground under your feet.

steps: Form both hands into F handshapes, joining thumb and index finger into a circle on each hand.
Hold both hands in front of your chest, a few inches apart, with fingertips pointed at each other.
Move the hands toward each other until the tips of the F handshapes touch lightly.
Keep the palms angled slightly inward, facing each other, throughout the motion.
Hold a calm, confident expression — the sign is a straightforward compliment.
tip: There is also a P-handshape version that touches middle fingertips instead — do not mix the two mid-sign.

steps: Raise your dominant hand beside your head, forming a loose open hand with the fingers slightly curved.
Bring the hand up to the side of your head, near the top where the hair sits.
Brush the hand downward along the side of your head, as if smoothing a lock of hair.
Keep the palm facing inward toward your head through the whole downward stroke.
Keep your expression neutral, and let the motion stay close to the head instead of floating out wide.
tip: Do not grip like holding a brush — an A-fist brushing down the head means HAIRBRUSH, not hair.

steps: Shape both hands into flat B handshapes, fingers together and pointing straight up.
Hold both hands in front of your chest with the upright fingertips nearly touching at the center.
Move the two hands outward to opposite sides, opening a wide flat span like a wall rising.
Keep the palms facing forward, away from your body, for the whole outward movement.
Hold a neutral expression and keep the hands at chest height; the sign simply depicts the flat surface.
tip: Widen or shrink the span to show a wall's size — the sign doubles as a size-and-shape classifier.

steps: Point both index fingers upward with your other fingers curled into loose fists.
Hold both hands in front of your torso at about chest height.
Twist your wrists as you trace two small upward arcs through the air.
Let each fingertip draw a loose cursive W shape, moving upward and outward.
Keep both palms angled toward each other with the fingers leading the motion.
Pair the sign with a bright, satisfied expression to show a good outcome.
tip: The two upward fingertip arcs sketch a cursive W — Lifeprint glosses this sign SUCCEED.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat and steady at chest height, palm facing down.
Raise your dominant hand slightly above and a few inches behind the base hand.
Keep the dominant hand in a flat shape with its palm angled downward.
Bring the dominant hand forward over the base hand in one quick motion.
End with a firm stop above the base hand, as if hitting an invisible ceiling.
Use a decisive facial expression — this sign marks a hard upper limit.
tip: Think of the moving hand smacking an invisible ceiling — that firm stop is the maximum.

steps: Start with your dominant hand a few inches in front of your chest.
Shape the hand like a loose grip, as if about to unscrew a light bulb.
Move the hand inward until the thumb side approaches your chest.
Close the fingers into a flattened O as the hand reaches your body.
End with the flat of your thumbnail touching your chest, fingertips meeting.
Keep a matter-of-fact expression; this sign claims possession of something.
tip: It grew out of the fingerspelled O-W-N — the flattened O lands on the chest.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand out as a flat five hand, palm facing sideways.
Reach over with your dominant hand and grasp the non-dominant fingers lightly.
Pull the grasped hand forward in a short, steady tug toward your front.
Release and repeat the pull once more to show more than one guide.
Keep both movements smooth and even, like leading someone by the hand.
Face the direction of travel with an attentive, helpful expression.
tip: One pull leads one person; the repeated tug marks the plural — people who lead.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into an R by crossing your middle finger over your index finger.
Touch the R-hand to one corner of your chin, palm facing inward.
Move the hand across to touch the other corner of your chin.
Repeat the chin-to-chin sweep once more to show more than one place.
Keep the palm facing inward toward your face through both short moves.
Use the same neutral expression as the eating signs — you are naming places to eat.
tip: Same mouth-corner path as EAT; the repeated sweep turns one restaurant into many.

steps: Form a loose four hand with your dominant hand, fingers together and thumb tucked.
Hold the hand beside your lower cheek, near the chin, palm facing sideways.
Shake the hand downward twice in two small, quick strokes.
Keep the strokes short — about an inch — right against the cheek.
Use a neutral expression; context separates this from the color brown.
Some signers circle a W handshape at the cheek instead — know both, use the common one.
tip: Lifeprint glosses WINE the same as BEER — two quick shakes beside the lower cheek.

steps: Press your fingertips against your thumb to form a flattened O handshape.
Bring the flattened O up beside one side of your nose.
Touch lightly as if holding a blossom under your nose to smell it.
Move the hand to the other side of your nose and touch again.
Keep the hand relaxed and the palm angled down toward the face.
Pair the sign with a pleasant expression, as if enjoying the scent.
tip: One touch smells a single flower; touching both sides of the nose shows many.

steps: Point both index fingers upward with your other fingers folded into fists.
Raise both hands to face level, in front of your eyes.
Slide the index fingers up and down past each other in an alternating rhythm.
Turn both palms to face forward, away from your face.
Look up at your hands and toward the imagined sky while you sign.
Repeat the rubbing motion several times to show many stars twinkling.
tip: The alternating finger-rub already suggests many; extra repeats make the plural clear.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand upright at chest height, fingers together and pointing up.
Turn that hand's palm sideways so it stands like a page of paper.
Bend the fingers of your dominant hand at the knuckles, forming a loose bent hand.
Touch the bent fingertips to the top edge of the upright paper hand.
Tap downward along the paper in steps, as if ticking items off a list.
Repeat the downward taps two or three times to show several separate lists.
tip: The base hand is the paper; repeated downward ticks mark each list's items.

steps: Hold your dominant hand in an upright U handshape, with the index and middle fingers extended together.
Keep your non-dominant hand flat and steady at chest height, palm facing downward.
Brush the wrist of the dominant U hand twice across the top of the non-dominant hand, like dusting a surface.
Angle the dominant palm slightly sideways so the U points backward as it slides across the base hand.
Keep your face neutral — the double brushing motion is part of the sign, not added emphasis.
tip: It shares the sign for USE — the two brush strokes mark the thing as worth using.

steps: Form an R handshape with your dominant hand by crossing the middle finger over the index finger.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat and upright at chest height, its palm facing toward your dominant hand.
Touch the dominant palm to the base palm, lift off slightly, slide down an inch, and touch the base palm again.
Keep the dominant palm facing the base palm through both contacts of the sign.
Hold a neutral, serious expression — this sign carries the weight of an official regulation.
tip: Same motion as LAW with an R hand — swap back to an L handshape and it reads as LAW instead.

steps: Shape both hands into loose 5 handshapes with the fingers spread and slightly bent.
Hold both hands up at chest height in front of your body, palms facing each other.
Point the fingertips of each hand toward the fingertips of the other hand, picturing lanes of cars.
Move the hands back and forth past each other in small alternating motions, like vehicles streaming in opposite lanes.
Keep the palms facing each other through the whole alternating movement.
Hold a matter-of-fact expression — the sign simply names the condition of traffic.
tip: The bent fingers are the lanes, not the cars — hands passing each other picture a busy multi-lane road.

steps: Extend the index finger of your dominant hand and point it straight down toward your own foot.
Hold the pointing hand low in front of your body so the fingertip aims at the ground near your feet.
Point first at one foot, then sweep your hand in a small arc and point at your other foot.
Keep your palm facing inward toward your body so the index finger stays vertical and clearly aimed downward.
Keep your face and body neutral, with your gaze following your hand down toward your feet.
tip: Sign feet with two quick points — using F hands like the shoe sign is Signed English, not ASL.

steps: Hold both hands in flat B handshapes with your thumbs resting alongside your fingers, not forming P shapes.
Raise both hands to the neutral signing space in front of your chest with your palms facing each other.
Move both hands straight downward a few inches together in one smooth, level motion.
Keep both palms facing inward toward each other and both hands moving evenly as they drop.
Keep your expression neutral and avoid any initialized P handshape when you use this sign alone.
tip: This flat-hands sign means person — attach it after a verb (TEACH plus AGENT) to say the person who does it, like teacher.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand in an open 5 handshape with all fingers spread in front of you.
Form a flat hand or a relaxed open 5 handshape with your dominant hand beside it.
Tap the thumb of your dominant hand against the tip of the non-dominant thumb, then tap it a second time.
Keep your non-dominant hand still and hold it slightly lower so the two thumb tips can meet.
Use this sign only for a school senior — a senior citizen uses a different established sign.
tip: Two taps on the opposite thumb mean a final-year student, never a senior citizen.

steps: Form both hands into flattened-O handshapes, with fingertips and thumbs rounded together.
Hold both hands up near your head, starting at about forehead height in front of you.
Push both hands forward away from your head, pull them slightly back, then push forward again in a double movement.
Keep your palms turned slightly inward toward each other as your hands travel outward.
Use the double movement only for the ongoing process of teaching; one quick movement means the verb teach.
tip: Single movement is the verb teach (I teach ASL); the double movement turns it into teaching as a process or profession.

steps: Hold your dominant hand flat in a B handshape and keep your non-dominant hand flat and still beside it.
Raise your dominant hand to chest height in front of you, starting with the palm facing forward.
Swing your dominant hand outward as if opening a door, then swing it back inward to close it, using two movements.
Keep your palm facing forward the whole time and let your pinkie-side edge act as the door's hinge.
Keep your face neutral; depending on context this same sign can also mean closet, cupboard, or cabinet.
tip: The hinge sits on your pinkie side — pivoting at the thumb edge is the common beginner mistake.

steps: Hold both hands in front of you with your index fingers extended straight and pointing upward.
Curl both index fingers into X handshapes as you begin moving both hands downward together.
Draw the path of a question mark in the air with your moving hands, then open both into palm-down 5 hands to dot it.
Keep your palms facing downward as the 5 handshapes finish the sign in the neutral signing space.
Maintain a thoughtful, inquisitive expression while the hands trace the question-mark shape.
tip: This one sign covers testing, a test, an exam, or a quiz — never swap in the TRY sign for phrases like test my patience.

steps: Form both hands into F handshapes by touching each thumb to its index fingertip.
Hold both F hands in front of you about eight inches apart at mid-chest height.
Move your right hand up a few inches while your left hand moves down the same distance at the same time.
Reverse the motion, bringing the right hand down as the left hand rises, like a balance scale tipping.
Hold your right palm facing left and your left palm facing right, and keep your expression serious and formal.
tip: Picture the scales of justice tipping back and forth — this same sign is also glossed judge, court, and if.

steps: Hold both hands in flat B handshapes with your fingers extended together and thumbs alongside.
Bring both hands into the neutral signing space in front of your body at chest height.
Sweep your dominant hand in a wide circular scooping motion across and around toward your non-dominant hand.
Start your dominant hand with the palm facing out and let it turn to face back as the scoop finishes.
Keep your non-dominant hand fairly still with its palm facing back, and keep your expression neutral unless emphasizing.
tip: This sign is also glossed all or whole — make the scoop bigger and wider to stress the whole thing, every bit of it.

steps: Hook your dominant index finger over your thumb to form an X handshape, folding the remaining fingers down.
Place the hooked X hand just under your chin, close to the front of your throat.
Flick the X hand forward about three inches with a quick wrist motion, then repeat the flick once more.
Angle your palm slightly downward so the hooked X points forward as it slides away from your throat.
Hold a neutral, matter-of-fact expression — this sign simply names the material.
tip: The same flicking X also signs steel — it covers the whole metal family.

steps: Extend the index fingers of both hands, folding the remaining fingers of each hand into loose fists.
Hold your non-dominant index finger sideways at chest height, pointing across your body like the bottom bar of a plus sign.
Cross your dominant index finger over it at a right angle, touching the fingers near their middles to draw a plus.
Keep both palms facing each other as the fingertips meet at the center of the cross.
Wear a calm, upbeat expression that matches the meaning of staying positive.
tip: This is the math-class PLUS sign doing double duty — picture adding a plus to your attitude.

steps: Spread the fingers of both hands wide into open five handshapes.
Raise both hands to chest height in front of you, with all the fingers pointing upward.
Push the hands together so the fingertips interlock, like two opposing scrimmage lines clashing at the snap.
Ram the hands together twice in a quick double movement, keeping the fingers meshed.
Keep the palms facing each other through both rams of the sign.
Hold a neutral, game-ready expression — the double clash is part of the sign.
tip: The fingers are the two scrimmage lines, not a ball — never shape the hands into a football.

steps: Curve the fingers of both hands into loose bent handshapes, with the fingertips pointing downward.
Raise both bent hands to the tops of your shoulders, close to your neck.
Touch the fingertips down onto your shoulders, then lift and touch again with a firm double tap.
Keep the palms angled inward toward your chest through both contacts.
Hold a steady, earnest expression — the repeated tap marks this as a duty.
tip: No R handshape needed — think of the weight of a duty resting on your shoulders.

steps: Pinch your thumb and index finger together with the other fingers folded to form the letter G, palm facing you.
Open into U by extending your index and middle fingers straight up together.
Curl all four fingertips down onto your thumb to form E, keeping your palm facing forward.
Close your hand into an S fist with your thumb lying across the front of your folded fingers.
Finish with T by tucking your thumb up between your index and middle fingers, flowing smoothly between letters.
Hold your hand at chest height and mouth the word 'guest' lightly as you spell.
tip: Signers fingerspell the word itself — then use invite or visit to show what the guest is doing.

steps: Raise your dominant hand in front of your face in a slightly cupped open handshape, fingers together and softly bent.
Hold the hand at about eye level, a few inches from your face, like a small hand mirror.
Twist your wrist once to turn the hand sideways, as if glancing around to form an impression.
Angle the palm toward yourself at the start of the twist, keeping the cupped shape steady.
Purse your lips and narrow your eyes slightly, as if thinking hard while you size things up.
tip: MIRROR uses the same handshape with a quick double tap and a neutral face; SEEM twists once with a thinking face.

steps: Form an F handshape with each hand, pressing each thumb tip against its index fingertip in a small ring.
Hook the two F hands together by linking the index finger and thumb of one hand through the ring of the other.
Hold the linked hands in front of your torso, near chest height, with the hands close together.
Rock the joined hands gently back and forth twice while keeping both F handshapes intact.
Keep your face neutral and your body still, letting the linked hands show the connection.
tip: The interlocked rings stand for two parties tied together; context decides whether you mean family ties or a relationship.

steps: Hold both hands in front of your torso in loosely clawed shapes, fingers curved with the dominant hand just above the other.
Let the two hands hover near each other, with the upper hand's palm angled slightly downward toward the lower one.
Shift both hands a few inches outward to the sides at the same time.
As the hands move apart, close each hand into a firm S fist, thumb resting over the curled fingers.
Hold a calm, sincere expression, as if resting steady confidence on the other person.
tip: Clawed hands close into S fists as they part — do not confuse it with CONFIDENCE, which uses a different movement.

steps: Hold both hands up in front of your torso with all fingers and thumbs spread loosely apart.
Bring the hands toward each other at chest height until the fingertips of both hands meet in the middle.
Tap the fingertips of both hands together once, as if many people are gathering into one group.
Angle the palms toward each other and slightly downward as the fingertips touch.
Keep a neutral, informative expression instead of the raised-eyebrow look of a question.
tip: All fingers meet for a group session; two index fingers alone would change it to a one-on-one 'meet'.

steps: Form a C handshape with your dominant hand, thumb and fingers curved as if around a camera lens.
Hold the C hand up beside your eye on your dominant side, about temple height.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat and upright in front of your chest, with its palm facing sideways toward the C hand.
Bring the C hand down so its open side lands against the upright non-dominant palm, as if capturing the image.
Keep both palms facing each other sideways during the contact, and keep your face neutral.
tip: This is the take-a-picture sign — context decides whether you mean the photo, the camera, or the craft itself.

steps: Relax both hands into open 5 handshapes, fingers together and slightly loose, with the thumbs ready.
Hold both hands at chest height with the thumbs aimed at your upper chest.
Poke your upper chest twice with both thumb tips, moving the hands forward and back with each poke.
Angle both palms inward toward your body so the thumbs can reach the chest squarely.
Keep your face relaxed and easy, matching the carefree time-off feeling.
tip: One poke usually means time off or spring break, two pokes a holiday; an R-handshape version of this sign means retired.

steps: Form a C handshape with your dominant hand, thumb and fingers curved open.
Hold the C in front of your body at chest height, slightly to your dominant side.
