Trace a quick small circle with the C hand, moving clockwise from your own point of view.
Keep the hand upright with the opening of the C facing outward toward your audience as you circle.
Mouth the word 'century' while signing, since viewers usually need the sentence context to catch it.
tip: Some signers shake the C side to side instead of circling; either way, mouthing 'century' is what makes it read clearly.

steps: Hold both hands in loose flat handshapes, fingers together with thumbs resting casually alongside.
Hold the non-dominant hand steady at chest height with its palm facing upward.
Bring the dominant hand down onto the non-dominant palm twice, as if clapping quietly.
Keep the dominant palm facing down and the base hand facing up as the hands meet.
Use a neutral, matter-of-fact expression, keeping most of the motion in the dominant hand.
tip: Same production as SCHOOL — context tells listeners whether you mean a school or the academic sense; it is not the sign for college.

steps: Close your dominant hand into a loose A fist, keeping the thumb sticking up and slightly out.
Rest that fist on the open palm of your flat non-dominant hand, held at about waist height.
Lift both hands upward together a few inches, as if boosting the fist from below.
Keep the non-dominant palm facing up so it visibly supports the raised fist.
Aim the sign toward the person you mean: start near yourself for 'I help you', near them for 'you help me'.
tip: HELP is directional — the lifting motion points at whoever receives the assistance, so no separate ME or YOU sign is needed.

steps: Close both hands into A fists, thumbs tucked firmly against the side of the curled fingers.
Press the two fists together in front of your chest, with their palms facing each other.
Slide your dominant fist backward so it moves directly behind the stationary non-dominant fist.
Keep the non-dominant fist held steady in place as the reference point for the movement.
Hold a neutral expression and keep the palms facing each other from start to finish.
tip: It belongs to the WITH sign family - join the A hands, then let the movement point the direction: back reads as behind.

steps: Flatten both hands with fingers together and thumbs tucked, palms facing the ground.
Raise the flat hands to about waist height, keeping them low in front of your body.
Touch the fingertips of the two hands together in the center to form one level plane.
Sweep both hands smoothly outward to the sides, spreading them wide like laying a surface.
Follow the sweep with your eyes and keep a neutral face, letting the wide flat motion carry the meaning.
tip: Lifeprint notes this also means carpet - picture smoothing a flat sheet across a room.

steps: Extend the index finger of your dominant hand and curl the remaining fingers shut.
Hold your non-dominant forearm flat and level in front of you, palm angled slightly downward.
Set the dominant index fingertip against the inside of the wrist and drag it steadily up the forearm.
Stretch the drag into one extra-long continuous pull so the extended movement itself means longer.
Watch the moving finger and slow the motion down; a bigger unhurried stroke reads as greater length.
tip: ASL compares by stretching the movement - a normal pull signs long, an extended pull signs longer.

steps: Form the letter N by folding the middle finger of your dominant hand over the thumb.
Hold the N hand at chest height with the fingers pointing up and the palm facing left.
Drive the whole hand straight upward several inches in one firm vertical stroke.
Keep the wrist straight through the lift so the movement reads as clearly upward.
End the stroke near chin level with a neutral face; upward on a map is the north you are naming.
tip: Think of a wall map - north sits at the top, so the N hand climbs upward for northern.

steps: Shape your non-dominant hand into a firm O and hold it upright at chest height.
Spread the fingers of your dominant hand, then bend the middle finger sharply at its largest knuckle.
Poke the bent middle finger into the opening of the non-dominant O hand.
Pull the finger back out and immediately slap your open dominant palm down over the O opening.
Make both the poke and the slap quick and snappy, since the sudden snap sells the fizzy idea.
tip: This is pop as in soda pop - mime the quick burst of a bottle opening for a cleaner production.

steps: Pinch your dominant thumb and fingers loosely together, as if gripping a thin matchstick.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat before your chest with the palm facing sideways and fingers up.
Strike the dominant fingertips downward across the base palm, like scratching a match to light it.
For the noun form, make two very small quick strikes instead of one sweeping stroke.
For the verb form, use one single large strike and keep your expression focused.
tip: This is the matchstick sense; matching two things as a pair belongs to the combine sign family.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into an F, thumb and index touching as if pinching a tiny ring.
Hold your non-dominant hand up with the fingers extended so the ring finger is easy to see.
Slide the F handshape down along the non-dominant ring finger, setting the imaginary band onto it.
Pause briefly with the F handshape resting at the base of the finger to show the ring in place.
Keep the non-dominant hand still and your face neutral, letting the F handshape tell the jewelry story.
tip: The F hand itself looks like a ring - pinch an imaginary band and slide it onto the finger.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat and open at chest height, fingers together and pointing forward.
Form an X handshape with your dominant hand by hooking the index finger over the thumb.
Move the dominant X hand firmly toward the open base palm until it makes contact.
Draw the X hand back toward your body slightly right after contact to complete the demand.
Keep your expression serious throughout; a firm face matches the weight of an obligation.
tip: It sits in the same family as NEED, with the X hand adding the force of something demanded.

steps: Form the letter A with both hands by closing each into a fist with the thumb beside the fingers.
Bring the two A fists together in front of your chest so they touch like a close pair.
Rock the joined hands forward and back together, about three inches in each direction.
Repeat the forward-back rock a second time so the pair moves as one steady unit.
Keep a warm relaxed expression, since the sign describes an ongoing romantic relationship.
tip: This is the GO-STEADY sign - it covers dating as a relationship, not one single date night.

steps: Hold your dominant hand in a loose open shape with the fingers relaxed and slightly spread.
Start the hand near your chest at mid-torso height, as if you are just inside a building.
Sweep the hand upward and outward in a rising arc toward the open space ahead of you.
Repeat the up-and-out sweep a second time with a quick beat to name the noun outdoors.
Aim your gaze toward the open space as you sign, since the eyes help mark the outside area.
tip: One big sweep says go out; doubling the movement names the place - outdoors.

steps: Form a P handshape with your dominant hand, tucking the thumb between the middle and index fingers with the palm facing down.
Hold the P hand out in neutral space in front of your chest, keeping it steady at chest height.
Move the hand in a small smooth circle, repeating the circling motion twice for emphasis.
Keep the palm facing downward throughout the entire circling movement.
Hold a neutral expression, since the initialized handshape and the circling motion carry the whole meaning.
tip: Think of circling a P in the air — in some contexts signers simply sign MEAT instead, so follow the conversation.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a flat O, pressing the fingertips together with the palm facing upward.
Slide the flat-O hand inside the loose C hand of your non-dominant hand, held in front of your chest.
Push the dominant hand upward out of the C hand, opening the fingers into a loose five hand as it rises.
Make the whole rising motion two times in small, quick repetitions — the doubled motion marks the noun.
Keep your palm facing up and your face relaxed, picturing a seedling shooting out of the soil.
tip: One smooth rising motion means the verb 'grow'; repeat it twice in small motions and it becomes the noun 'plant'.

steps: Open both hands into relaxed five handshapes, keeping the fingers loosely spread and natural.
Lift both arms and cross them over your chest, the right hand coming to rest near the left shoulder.
Land both open hands gently on your shoulders or upper chest as the crossed arms settle into place.
Keep your palms facing inward toward your own body while the arms stay folded.
Soften your shoulders and relax your expression, as if settling in for a quiet pause.
tip: The folded arms picture taking a break — hold the hands loose and keep the sign still and calm.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into an index-finger handshape, pointing with the tip of the finger.
Raise the hand to face level and aim the index fingertip toward one of your eyes.
Hold the pointing finger close to the eye without touching it, keeping the motion small and clear.
Angle your palm inward and keep it steady so the finger points straight at the eye.
Look straight ahead with a neutral face, letting the pointing gesture do all the talking.
tip: To sign 'eyes' in the plural, point to each eye in turn — the pointing itself is the whole sign.

steps: Bend your dominant index finger into a hooked shape, keeping the remaining fingers closed.
Raise the hand to the side of your head, holding it near the temple.
Tap the hooked fingertip twice against the side of your head with a small, crisp motion.
Keep your palm facing inward toward your head throughout both taps.
Pair the sign with a slightly puzzled or neutral expression, matching a 'does that make sense?' question.
tip: This is the 'does that make sense?' sense — a hooked finger tapping the temple twice.

steps: Form an F handshape with your dominant hand, touching the thumb and index finger into a small circle.
Touch the F hand to one side of your chest, making clear and deliberate contact.
Lift the hand and move it across to the other side of your chest, touching again — never drag it.
Keep the palm facing inward toward your chest at both contact points.
Hold a neutral, professional expression and keep the two taps crisp and even.
tip: It rides on the same chest-tap pattern as MEMBER — the F handshape is what makes it faculty.

steps: Form a P handshape with your dominant hand, holding it so the index finger points upward.
Point the hand toward your temple, with the tip of the middle finger close to the side of your head.
Draw a small circle in the air with the hand, then end the motion by touching the temple.
Keep the palm facing inward so the middle fingertip makes the final contact on the head.
Use a neutral, serious expression, matching the formal tone of the topic.
tip: An initialized GOVERNMENT — the P hand circles in the air and lands on the temple.

steps: Bend the fingers of both hands at the two smaller knuckles, keeping the hands relaxed and natural.
Hold both hands in front of your chest, palms facing each other a few inches apart.
Bring the hands together twice, letting the fingers meet lightly each time.
Keep your palms facing each other and the movement even and unhurried.
Use a warm, neutral expression — the joining motion shows two people pairing up.
tip: The same sign as ROOMMATE; for a romantic partner many signers also use SHARE-PERSON.

steps: Cup your non-dominant hand loosely and hold it in front of your waist as a container.
Hold your dominant hand flat above it, fingers together, as if carrying items to put inside.
Bring your dominant hand down and tuck it into the cupped hand, pressing the items in.
Repeat the pressing-down motion once more to show packing things firmly together.
Keep the hands angled toward each other during the tucking motion.
Keep a neutral face; the sign reads like physically filling a box or bag.
tip: Think of stuffing clothes into a suitcase — the top hand presses goods into the bottom hand's box.

steps: Hold your non-dominant forearm horizontally across your body with the palm facing down.
Make a flat hand with your dominant hand, fingers extended and held together.
Place the edge of your dominant hand on the forearm, close to your body.
Sweep your dominant flat hand outward along the top of the forearm.
Keep the palm facing down the whole time so the hand reads as a flat platform.
Keep your body still and your expression neutral throughout the sign.
tip: Your sweeping flat hand becomes the raised platform — one common variant spreads two bent hands outward instead.

steps: Make both hands flat, fingers extended and together, with palms facing upward.
Hold the hands in front of your chest, side by side, a few inches apart.
Move both hands forward and slightly upward in one smooth arc.
Let the hands dip slightly downward at the end of the arc, as if setting something on a table.
Keep both palms facing the ceiling from the start of the sign to the finish.
Pair it with a warm, open expression, as though offering someone an idea.
tip: Picture yourself laying an offer on the table — this is the same sign as SUGGEST and OFFER.

steps: Make both hands into fists with the thumbs extended upward.
Hold the hands in front of your chest, one hand slightly ahead of the other.
Slide the hands forward and back alternately, trading which hand leads.
Repeat the alternating motion a few times, like runners trading the lead.
Keep your thumbs pointing up and your palms facing each other.
Use an energetic face; this sign means a contest, not a person's heritage.
tip: The hands race each other back and forth — for heritage or ethnicity, spell R-A-C-E instead.

steps: Make an A handshape with your dominant hand, thumb pressed against the fist.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of your chest, palm facing upward.
As your dominant hand drops toward the flat palm, open it into a P handshape.
Slap the P hand firmly down into the open palm in one clean motion.
Finish with your dominant palm facing down into the flat base hand.
Nod slightly as you sign to show the stamp of agreement.
tip: The A-to-P handshape change slapped into the palm reads like a rubber stamp of approval.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you with the palm facing upward.
With your dominant hand, form the letter B and touch it to the open palm.
Change the dominant hand to the letter G and tap it onto the palm.
Keep the two letters close together, spelling B-G in one flowing motion.
Keep the base palm steady and facing the ceiling while you spell.
Use a matter-of-fact expression; the sign means personal history or context.
tip: It is an initialized sign — just spell B-G onto the palm to mean someone's background.

steps: Make a flat hand with your dominant hand, fingers extended and held together.
Hold the flat hand against your upper chest, near the center.
Slide the hand slowly downward along the front of your torso.
End the motion around your mid-chest or stomach area.
Keep your palm facing toward your body as the hand descends.
Wear a neutral, thoughtful expression, as though describing someone's nature.
tip: The hand traces down through the body — this sign means personality, not a written letter.

steps: Make both hands into A handshapes, with thumbs resting against the fists.
Hold the fists up near your shoulders, a few inches from your body.
Thrust both fists downward together in a short, firm motion.
Repeat the downward thrust once more to show established ability.
Keep your palms facing downward or inward through the movement.
Hold your head high with a confident expression as you sign it.
tip: Same sign as CAN — the two fists dropping down together signal capability.

steps: Make both hands flat, fingers extended and held together.
Hold the hands apart in neutral space in front of your waist.
Tilt the hands up and down alternately, like the two sides of a balance scale.
Repeat the seesaw motion a couple of times without pausing.
Keep both palms facing upward throughout the tilting.
Shrug your shoulders slightly and raise your eyebrows to show uncertainty.
tip: The palms-up hands seesaw like an old-fashioned balance scale weighing yes against no.

steps: Make both hands flat, fingers extended and held together.
Hold the hands out in front of your body, off to your dominant side.
Sweep both hands together toward your non-dominant side, as if carrying a load.
Repeat the carrying sweep to show the ongoing act of moving.
Keep both palms facing downward as the hands travel across.
Look in the direction the hands travel, like watching boxes being carried.
tip: The hands carry an imaginary load from one side to the other — it covers relocating house, not just motion.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a relaxed open five with the fingers spread softly.
Hold the hand in front of your cheek with the fingertips pointing up near your chin.
Move the hand outward and away from your face while turning your wrist.
Let the fingertips draw together into a pinched handshape as the hand travels outward.
Keep the palm facing mostly toward you until the wrist begins its turn.
Smile gently as you sign, since a warm expression belongs to this sign.
tip: Do not mix it up with LOOKS — PRETTY ends with the fingertips pinched together after the outward twist.

steps: Close your dominant hand into an S, fist shut with the thumb over the fingers.
Hold the S hand in front of your chest at about shoulder height.
Move the hand straight downward several inches, as if following a map downward.
Keep the palm facing toward your non-dominant side through the whole drop.
Use one smooth motion and keep your face neutral for a plain direction.
tip: Some signers do SOUTH palm-down instead — either version is understood; think of pointing toward the bottom of a map.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into an A, fist closed with the thumb sticking up.
Point the thumb toward the person you are talking about, arm extended.
Thrust the hand toward that person, pull back about an inch, then thrust again.
Keep the A handshape firm and make the motion a short double jab.
Raise your eyebrows when asking 'how about YOURSELF?' to mark the question.
tip: Aim the sign at the person it means — YOURSELF always points at your listener, never at you.

steps: Form your non-dominant hand into an S and hold it steady in front of you.
Shape your dominant hand into an open five, fingers together, palm down.
Press the dominant hand down onto the S hand, pushing it downward.
Repeat the downward press once more, for a total of two presses.
Keep the base hand fixed in place while the top hand does the pushing.
Show a little tension in your face and shoulders, as if straining.
tip: Use one press and the meaning shifts toward oppression — always use two presses for PRESSURE.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you with the palm facing up.
Extend the index finger of your dominant hand and close the other fingers.
Jab the fingertip down into the upturned palm like pointing at an amount due.
Repeat the jab once more, for a total of two firm downward pokes.
Keep the palm hand steady and flat while the dominant hand does the jabbing.
Hold a serious expression, as if reminding someone of money owed.
tip: Two jabs make the noun DEBT; a single jab leans toward the verb OWE.

steps: Shape your non-dominant hand into a flat hand, fingers together, palm down.
Shape your dominant hand into a flat hand too, holding it above the base hand.
Slide the dominant hand back and forth across the base hand like sawing.
Use a double movement — two sawing strokes — to name the material WOOD.
Keep the sawing hand's palm facing down as it moves across the log.
Watch the base hand while you sign, like following the saw's cut.
tip: The flat base hand is the log and the moving hand is the saw — two strokes mark the noun WOOD.

steps: Shape both hands into loose five handshapes with the fingers softly spread.
Hold both hands in front of your chest with the palms facing your body.
Pull both hands inward toward your chest in one smooth motion.
Close the fingertips toward the thumbs, finishing in eight handshapes.
End the pull near the middle of your chest, palms still facing in.
Raise your eyebrows and lean in slightly, as if showing real curiosity.
tip: It is a two-handed LIKE pulled to the chest — sign it with one hand and it only means LIKE.

steps: Shape both hands into flat open hands with fingertips together, like the starting position of the PLEASE sign.
Place your right flat hand on your upper chest and your left flat hand on your belly, an inch or two out from your body.
Circle both hands at the same time in opposite directions, with the right hand looping clockwise and the left hand counterclockwise.
Angle your palms inward toward your torso so the fingertips of each hand point toward the other hand.
Wear a warm, content smile while signing, since the sign conveys pleasure and delight.
tip: Same motion as PLEASE done with both hands — this production also means APPRECIATE.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you with the palm facing up.
Hover your dominant hand above it in a loose, relaxed open shape with the palm facing down.
Sweep your dominant hand toward your flat palm, close it into a fist as it touches, then pull it away.
Let the dominant hand drop slightly and reopen into a loose open hand, still palm down.
Keep the palm-down orientation through the whole motion — the hand only opens and closes, it never turns over.
tip: Think of grabbing something off a surface and letting it drop — Lifeprint uses this same sign in ELIMINATE.

steps: Form both hands into Y handshapes, extending your thumbs and pinkies while folding the middle fingers down.
Raise both Y hands into the signing space in front of your chest.
Shake both hands side to side repeatedly with a loose, playful motion.
Turn your palms inward so they face toward each other as the hands shake.
Keep an animated, cheerful expression to match the sense of ongoing fun.
tip: The repeated shake IS the 'playing' — Lifeprint warns never to initialize this sign with P handshapes.

steps: Extend your non-dominant hand in front of you in a flat handshape, palm facing up.
Shape your dominant hand into the letter X, hooking your index finger with the palm facing back toward you.
Bring the top of your hooked index finger down onto your flat palm with one firm downward tap.
Keep the striking hand palm-back as it lands on your non-dominant palm.
Use a neutral, businesslike expression, as if naming a price.
tip: This is the COST sign — Lifeprint glosses it for cost, fee, fine, worth, and value.

steps: Start READ by extending your dominant index and middle fingers, holding them like two eyes scanning a page.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you to act as the page being read.
Move your two reading fingertips downward once along the flat page hand.
Finish with the AGENT marker: hold both hands flat with palms facing inward toward your torso.
Move both flat hands downward together past your chest to name 'a person who reads'.
Keep a neutral expression while the AGENT suffix does the grammatical work.
tip: READ plus the AGENT suffix — the exact verified pattern Lifeprint uses for TEACHER.

steps: Hold your dominant hand steady in the signing space with your palm facing outward.
Form the letter V, then transition smoothly through I, R, T, U, A, and L in sequence.
Keep each letter crisp but flowing, without pausing or bouncing the hand.
Face your palm outward for the whole spelling, the standard fingerspelling orientation.
Spell at a calm, readable pace so the English word stays recognizable.
tip: Lifeprint notes VIRTUAL is most often just fingerspelled — there is no widely used dedicated sign.

steps: Hold your dominant hand in the signing space with your palm facing outward to fingerspell.
Spell R-E-N-T crisply in sequence, forming each letter clearly and smoothly.
Keep your hand still in one spot, letting only the fingers change shape between letters.
Face your palm outward the whole time, the standard fingerspelling orientation.
Sign at a calm, readable pace so the word stays clear to your conversation partner.
tip: Fingerspelling R-E-N-T is what most signers use; every-MONTH can mean 'rent' when context is clear.

steps: Hold your dominant hand near the side of your forehead with your fingers extended and relaxed.
Touch or hover at your temple, just beside your forehead.
Wiggle your fingers in one small fluttering movement; a single wiggle is enough.
Prefer this non-initialized version over the T-handshape variant, which some signers still use.
Wear a thoughtful, serious expression, matching the weight of an abstract idea.
tip: Same family as IDEA at the forehead — but the fingers wiggle in place instead of pulling out like a light bulb.

steps: Make a fist with your dominant hand, keeping the thumb extended upward like a thumbs-up.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you with the palm facing upward.
Rest the dominant fist on top of the open non-dominant palm, keeping contact between them.
Lift both hands upward together in one smooth motion, as if raising support to someone.
Keep a warm, open expression that matches the idea of offering assistance.
tip: Signs exactly like HELP — the fist of effort lifted up off an open palm.

steps: Bend the fingers of your dominant hand into a loose bent handshape, keeping the palm facing downward.
Hold your non-dominant hand still in front of your chest with the palm facing down as a fixed reference point.
Start the dominant hand just below and slightly behind the non-dominant hand.
Twist or sweep the dominant hand forward past the reference hand, ending with a firm, definite stop.
Keep a neutral, matter-of-fact expression — this sign simply sets a lower limit.
tip: One of the 'than' family — the forward twist with a hard stop draws a floor under the amount.

steps: Bend the fingers of both hands downward into loose bent handshapes.
Hold both hands up in front of your chest with the fingertips pointing toward each other.
Bring the fingertips of both hands together until they nearly meet in the middle.
Keep both palms facing inward toward each other, not angled downward, as the fingers come together.
Use a neutral, even expression — this sign also covers the senses of equal and level.
tip: Lifeprint glosses this EQUAL-[fair, level] — the inward palms and meeting fingertips picture balance.

steps: Hook your dominant index finger over your thumb to form an X handshape, folding the remaining fingers down.
Place the hooked X hand just under your chin, close to the front of your throat.
Flick the X hand forward about three inches with a quick motion of the wrist.
Repeat the forward flick one more time, for a total of two quick flicks.
Keep your palm angled slightly downward as the hand flicks away from your throat.
Hold a neutral, matter-of-fact expression — this sign simply names the material.
tip: The same flicking X signs METAL — Lifeprint lists it as the sign for 'metal / ore / steel'.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand out flat with the fingers together, except for the middle and index fingers.
Position your dominant hand so its index finger points at the base of the other hand's middle and index fingers.
Touch the tip of the dominant index finger to the spot where those two fingers meet.
Twist the dominant hand with a small turning motion, as if turning a key.
Keep the twisting finger's palm facing sideways and your expression alert and ready.
tip: The twist is small and crisp — the same sign is taught as START, and a big twist would look like a different sign.

steps: Raise both hands in front of your chest with the index fingers pointing straight up and all other fingers curled down.
Hold your hands about shoulder-width apart at chest height, keeping the fingertips aimed toward the ceiling.
Sweep both index fingers in one fast, powerful arc upward, finishing with the fingertips well above shoulder level.
Keep your palms facing each other sideways while your fingertips trace the single rising arc.
Shape your mouth as if saying "pah" with a quick burst of air as your hands shoot upward.
tip: PAH! is the triumphant "at last, I did it" — not the sequencing word in "finally, thirdly."

steps: Hold both hands open in front of your torso with the fingers together and extended, not spread.
Rest your non-dominant hand palm-up a little below and forward, with your dominant hand palm-down hovering just above it.
Flip both hands sideways in one smooth motion so the top hand ends palm-up and the bottom hand ends palm-down.
Let the hands rotate past each other freely, keeping the fingers straight and relaxed through the turn.
Wear a somber, respectful expression that matches the seriousness of the topic.
tip: Many Deaf signers soften this with the GONE euphemism in context — use DEAD for direct statements.

steps: Form an "R" handshape with your dominant hand by crossing your middle finger over your index finger.
Place the R hand at your forehead with the fingertips near your temple, like saluting an idea.
Move your hand forward and slightly outward away from your forehead in one smooth, deliberate motion.
Keep your palm facing sideways toward your other side as the hand travels forward through the air.
Pair the movement with a sincere, dignified expression when honoring someone's worth or status.
tip: Think of it as the honor motion made with an R hand — respect travels forward from the mind.

steps: Bend the fingers of your dominant hand into a relaxed curved shape, keeping your thumb extended.
Hold the curved hand at chest height in the signing space in front of your torso.
Sweep the hand in one big arching movement, pushing forward and over toward your non-dominant side.
Keep your palm angled downward through the whole arc, like skimming over a hilltop.
Watch along the path of the movement, as if following your own journey.
tip: Lifeprint glosses this TRAVEL for trip, journey, and tour — one big arc means a single trip; looping arcs mean traveling around.

steps: Shape both hands into F handshapes, pressing each thumb against its index fingertip.
Hold both F hands in front of your chest with the fingertips nearly touching.
Tap the two F hands together twice at the fingertips, using small crisp taps.
Turn your palms to face each other so the fingertips meet edge to edge.
Keep a thoughtful, appraising expression, as if weighing the value of something.
tip: This is the tail end of the sign IMPORTANT — Lifeprint glosses it for worth and value; use the COST sign for prices and fees.

steps: Shape both hands into flat open hands with your thumbs extended along the edges.
Stack your dominant flat hand on top of your non-dominant flat hand at chest height.
Slide the two hands apart diagonally — the top hand moves up and out, the lower hand down and out.
Turn your palms to face each other as the hands separate, like laying out steps.
Keep a calm, methodical expression, matching the orderly sense of the sign.
tip: One sign covers procedure, process, and pace — the separating hands lay out the steps of the procedure.

steps: Extend the fingers of your dominant hand together in a flat, relaxed shape.
Touch your fingertips lightly to your lips, as if checking for something to eat.
Pull the hand straight down a few inches, closing it into a tight fist as it drops.
Keep your palm facing inward toward your body through the whole downward pull.
Wear a somber, downcast expression — the sign carries real weight, so sign it with gravity.
tip: Fingertips at the mouth, then an empty fist pulled down — also glossed POVERTY and PAUPER.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a V, extending your index and middle fingers with the rest folded down.
Raise the V to face level, holding it just in front of your face.
Point the two fingertips at one eye, then shift the hand to point at your other eye.
Angle your palm inward so the V fingertips aim straight at each eye.
Look straight ahead with a neutral face, letting the pointing motion do the work.
tip: The V stands in for the two eyes — the EYE entry uses a single pointing finger for the singular.

steps: Bend the fingers of both hands into loose hooks, like two clasps ready to link.
Bring both hooked hands together at mid-chest, interlocking the fingers of one hand with the other.
Slide the linked hands back and forth against each other in a short cooperative sawing motion.
Keep your palms facing each other while the hooked fingers stay interlocked.
Hold a warm, engaged expression — the sign also means COOPERATION, so show the teamwork.
tip: Lifeprint teaches this for relationship and cooperation alike — linked fingers are the bond; the back-and-forth is the working together.

steps: Close both hands into fists and hold them at chest height in front of you.
Rest the wrist of your dominant fist on top of your non-dominant wrist.
Tap the dominant fist down onto the other wrist two or three times — this is WORK.
Open both hands flat with palms facing inward, then move them straight down past your chest together.
Keep your face neutral and steady; the flat-hands-down finish is the AGENT marker meaning a person who.
tip: WORK plus the AGENT suffix — the same sign covers singular worker and plural workers; context sets the number.

steps: Open your dominant hand with your thumb sticking out to the side.
Touch your thumb to one side of your chin, letting your fingers spread across your jaw.
Wipe the thumb across your chin to the other side in one smooth motion, like wiping away sweat.
Keep your palm angled inward toward your body through the whole wipe.
Hold a matter-of-fact expression — this is a plain noun, not an insult.
tip: Think of a farmer wiping his chin — Lifeprint's own memory aid. Do not fling the hand outward; that would be SLOPPY, a different sign.

steps: Interlace the fingers of both hands together, clasping them into one settled bundle.
Hold the clasped hands at mid-chest, a few inches out from your body.
Keep the hands still and quiet — there is no travel; the stillness is the meaning.
Let your palms face each other while the fingers stay interlaced.
Soften your face into a calm, serene expression with relaxed shoulders.
tip: Settled, clasped hands — the same sign means CALM and to PACIFY, as in bringing peace.

steps: Shape both hands into flat open hands with the fingers together and extended.
Hold your non-dominant flat hand steady at chest height in front of you.
Rest your dominant flat hand just above it, then sweep it in a small arc over the top, as if smoothing the school grounds.
Keep both of your palms facing downward through the whole sweeping arc.
Use a calm, neutral expression, like a guide describing the school grounds.
tip: The flat hands map the grounds — also glossed SCHOOL GROUNDS.

steps: Hold your dominant hand flat with your fingers together and extended.
Raise the hand to the side of your forehead, just beside your temple.
Flutter your fingers in place with small quick wiggles, letting the fingertips shimmer.
Angle your palm toward your non-dominant side as the fingers wiggle.
Wear a bright, inventive expression — the sign lives at the seat of ideas.
tip: A wiggling hand at the forehead — also glossed IMAGINE, INVENT, and MAKE BELIEVE.

steps: Curve the fingers of your dominant hand into a C shape, thumb opposite your fingertips.
Hold the C hand at chest height in front of your torso.
Close the C down into a fist in one smooth motion, letting the fingers curl shut.
Keep your palm angled inward toward your body as the hand closes.
Keep your face neutral and descriptive, as if naming a place on a map.
tip: The open C closes shut at your chest — fingerspelling C-O-A-S-T is also widely used for this word.

steps: Shape your non-dominant hand into a 1 handshape, holding your index finger upright and steady.
Raise that hand to chest height in front of your torso, keeping the finger pointing at the ceiling.
Close your dominant hand into a fist and tap it straight down onto the upright fingertip, like pinpointing a target.
Keep the dominant palm facing inward toward your body as the fist strikes downward.
Set your face in a firm, decisive expression, matching the precision the sign conveys.
tip: The downward tap pins the exact point — also glossed PINPOINT and GET TO THE POINT.

steps: Shape both hands into flat open hands with your thumbs extended along the edges.
Stack your dominant flat hand on top of your non-dominant flat hand at chest height.
Slide the two hands apart diagonally — the top hand moves up and out, the lower hand down and out.
Turn your palms to face each other as the hands separate, like stages moving forward.
Keep a steady, forward-looking expression, matching the sense of moving ahead.
tip: The same sign as PROCEDURE and PROCESS — the separating hands lay out the stages; context picks the English word.

steps: Curl both index fingers into hooked "X" handshapes, like loose fists with only the index fingers bent.
Hold the hooked hands near your chest with your palms facing upward toward the recipient.
Move both hands forward and slightly downward in one smooth arc, as if bestowing something on another person.
Keep your palms angled upward through the movement, ending with both hands extended forward.
Wear a serious, formal facial expression that matches the official tone of granting an award.
tip: This is the formal version of GIVE — the hooked X-hands carry the weight of 'confer,' 'bestow,' or 'award.'

steps: Touch your dominant index finger to your temple with your palm facing inward, like the sign for thinking.
Hook both index fingers and bring your dominant hand down to meet your non-dominant hand.
Let the two hooked fingers touch and interlock briefly in front of your chest.
Nod your head once as the hands meet, confirming 'yes, we are in agreement.'
Keep both palms angled toward each other and hold a positive, confirming facial expression.
tip: Think THINK-SAME: you tap your temple, then the two hooked index fingers meet — the head nod seals the agreement.

steps: Point your dominant index finger toward your face, holding it a few inches from your nose.
Sweep the index finger sideways past your nose in one smooth motion without ever touching it.
Keep your palm facing sideways and your finger held rigid as it crosses in front of your face.
Drive the movement from your wrist or elbow in a single confident pass across the midline.
Pair the sign with a neutral face, and add the INVENT sign for 'invented story' when you need extra clarity.
tip: Fiction borrows the FALSE sign — a story that is not true. For first reference, fingerspell F-I-C-T-I-O-N and add INVENT.

steps: Bend your dominant index finger into a slight hook, like a small tapping finger.
Tap the side of your ear twice with the tip of your hooked index finger.
Keep your palm facing outward and your elbow relaxed at your side while you tap.
Use a light, quick double-tap right at the ear opening for a clean production.
Keep your face neutral and your eyes on your conversation partner.
tip: Do not confuse it with LISTEN — hearing is a quick double-tap on the ear, listening holds an open hand cupped behind it.

steps: Raise both hands to chest height in loose, open '5' handshapes with your palms facing each other.
Move both hands forward and outward from your chest in a smooth, symmetrical twin motion.
As the hands travel forward, fold each middle finger down to touch its thumb, forming '8' handshapes.
Keep your palms angled inward toward each other through the entire movement.
Wear an engaged, curious facial expression with slightly raised eyebrows.
tip: It is a two-handed version of LIKE — the 5-to-8 handshape change as the hands move forward is the giveaway.

steps: Make a fist with your dominant hand and extend your thumb straight upward.
Hold the hand at chest height with the back of your hand facing outward.
Give the thumb a small side-to-side wiggle or a slight twist of the wrist.
Keep the other fingers tucked firmly into the fist while the thumb moves.
Hold a neutral, clear facial expression so the number reads cleanly.
tip: The little thumb wiggle is what separates the number ten from a plain thumbs-up.

steps: Hold both hands in flat 'B' handshapes with all fingers extended and pressed together.
Place your non-dominant hand in front of you with its palm facing toward your dominant side.
Rest your dominant hand lightly on top of the base hand with its palm facing the opposite way.
Slide only your dominant hand forward off the base hand in one smooth motion.
Keep the base hand still and finish with the moving hand extended ahead of it.
tip: This is the MAJOR sign — Lifeprint lists 'career' and 'profession' among its core meanings, so the same sign covers both.

steps: Curl your dominant hand into a loose fist, as if gripping a short pencil.
Touch the fist to your mouth, like wetting a pencil tip before taking notes.
Bring the fist down onto the flat, upturned palm of your non-dominant hand.
Mime quick writing strokes across that open palm, as if writing on paper.
Keep the non-dominant palm level and facing up while the fist writes on it.
Hold a calm, attentive expression, like someone taking dictation from a boss.
tip: Wet-the-pencil, then write on your palm: the sign pictures old-school dictation. Several versions exist — match your local Deaf community.

steps: Close both hands into loose fists, resting your thumbs across the top.
Hold the fists at chest height, about a shoulder-width apart in neutral space.
Turn both palms to face each other so the fists mirror one another.
Push both fists straight forward together in one smooth, level motion.
Freeze the fist shapes as they travel, like paving a stretch of road.
Keep your face neutral — this one sign covers street, way, path, and road.
tip: Two fists pushing forward pave the way — Lifeprint teaches street, way, path, and road as one shared sign.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand out flat, spreading only the index and middle fingers.
Place your dominant index finger at the base of those two spread fingers.
Twist the dominant index finger once, as if turning a small key.
Let the twisting finger's palm face sideways during the turning motion.
Wear an alert, ready expression that matches a fresh beginning.
tip: One small twist starts it all — Lifeprint: begin and start share this sign, so a big twist will look like a different word.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into an open hand with the thumb extended outward.
Touch your thumb firmly against the side of your forehead near the temple.
Sweep your hand straight down until the thumb lands flat on your chest.
Keep your palm angled toward your opposite side while the hand travels downward.
Hold a neutral, matter-of-fact expression, since the sign needs no special facial grammar.
tip: Lifeprint glosses this one sign as MAN, BOY, GUY, DUDE and FELLOW — context picks the English word.

steps: Shape both hands into loose open-F handshapes, each thumb tip resting against its index fingertip.
Hold your hands apart in the signing space in front of your chest.
Bring both hands toward each other and hook the fingers together into interlocking F shapes.
Angle your palms toward each other so the hooked fingers cross like two chain links.
End with a brief firm hold, adding a small nod when used as a statement.
tip: The same sign also covers JOIN, OF, MEMBER and OWN — let the sentence decide which English word fits.

steps: Hold both hands in slightly curved B handshapes, thumbs resting alongside the palms.
Start low in front of your torso with the fingertips of both hands nearly touching at the center.
Sweep both hands upward and outward in matching arcs to outline the basket's widening sides.
Keep your palms facing inward toward each other through the whole tracing motion.
Finish with your hands apart at roughly shoulder width, glancing at the shape you outlined.
tip: Scale the sign to the basket — a tall laundry hamper gets the same motion drawn taller and narrower.

steps: Form your dominant hand into an index-finger handshape with the other fingers folded down.
Hold your non-dominant hand out in front of you, flat and palm up, as a base.
Slide your dominant index finger forward across the base palm from wrist toward fingertips.
Without pausing, repeat the same forward slide across the palm a second time.
Keep the dominant palm facing down during both passes and a neutral expression.
tip: Repeating the sign turns WEEK into WEEKLY — ASL marks 'every' by doubling time signs.

steps: Hold both hands flat with the fingers together and palms facing each other.
Raise both hands to the sides of your head near your ears, like blinders on a horse.
Push both hands a short distance forward and away from your head.
Keep your palms facing inward toward each other through the whole forward push.
Direct a steady gaze toward the person you are addressing to reinforce the meaning.
tip: Reverse the direction — pull toward your own face — when you are calling for someone to pay attention to you.

steps: Raise both hands with the index fingers extended and the other fingers folded into fists.
Start at the top-left corner of the shape in the signing space before your chest.
Trace the outline of a square: right, then down, then left, then back up.
Keep your fingertips pointing forward and your palms angled slightly toward each other.
Use a confident neutral expression, mouthing the word lightly only if it helps clarity.
tip: The same sign also means BOARD and BILLBOARD — the sentence tells listeners which one you mean.

steps: Close both hands into fists with your thumbs resting against the fingers, forming A handshapes.
Hold your right fist near your chest and your left fist beside your abdomen, both a couple of inches off your body.
Thump both fists onto your body at the same time, bouncing them out and back in with a double in-out-in motion.
Keep your palms facing your body and your elbows relaxed as both hands land together.
Wear a straight, serious expression — the sign pictures a soldier gripping a rifle across the body.
tip: Think of two hands clapping a rifle against the body — the double thump is the signature; one thump is not enough.

steps: Open both hands flat with your fingers together and extended, palms angled upward and slightly toward each other.
Hold both hands in front of your chest, about a foot apart, at mid-chest height.
Push both hands smoothly forward and outward from your body in one short, decisive motion.
Let your palms turn to face fully upward as the hands travel, as if handing over permission.
Nod once with an open, granting expression — the sign should feel like opening a door for someone.
tip: It can take an initial P to mean permission — without the P it reads as allow or let.

steps: Hold your non-dominant index finger upright in front of your chest as a steady base.
Raise your dominant index finger above it with the other fingers folded down.
Bring the dominant index finger straight down so its tip lands firmly on the non-dominant index finger.
Keep both palms angled inward so the fingers meet tip to tip, not sideways.
Give a single confident nod as the fingers touch — you are confirming, not guessing.
tip: This covers accurate and right; the correcting-papers sense uses the criticizing CANCEL sign instead.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a loose N: fold your index and middle fingers down over your tucked thumb.
Close your non-dominant hand into a fist and hold it steady in front of your chest.
Move the N hand in one clockwise circle in the air just above the fist.
Set the N hand down firmly on the back of the fist, like planting a flag.
Keep your face composed and official — this is a formal word, not a casual one.
tip: NORMAL looks nearly identical — give NATION the deliberate plant-the-flag landing and keep NORMAL looser and quicker.

steps: Bend the fingers of both hands at the base joints and touch each thumb to its finger pads, making flattened O shapes.
Hold both hands close to your body at chest height, as if holding goods you are offering.
Push both hands straight forward away from your body in a smooth looping motion, and repeat the push to show the trade continuing.
Keep both palms angled slightly down as the hands cycle forward.
Face your imaginary customer with a businesslike, friendly, and open expression.
tip: SELLING is SELL done continuously — one clean push reads as sell, the repeated looping push reads as an ongoing trade.

steps: Relax both hands into loose fives with your fingers spread softly apart, not stiff.
Hold both hands in front of your body at chest height, tilted so the fingertips point a little upward.
Sweep both hands outward and slightly up in one smooth motion, as if showing the size of a pile.
Keep your palms angled toward each other through the whole outward sweep.
Widen your eyes and nod with emphasis — a lot is more than regular, and your face should say so.
tip: LOTS is BIG with relaxed hands and a more upward aim — it works for uncountable amounts, like a lot of rain.

steps: Touch your dominant thumb to your ring finger, pressing them firmly together.
Extend your other three fingers straight upward while the thumb and ring finger stay joined.
Hold the hand up in front of your shoulder in the neutral signing space.
Face your palm outward toward the person you are signing to.
Hold the handshape perfectly still with a neutral expression — the number itself does the talking.
tip: Numbers 6 through 9 each pin the thumb to a different finger: pinky is six, ring is seven, middle is eight, index is nine.

steps: Sign OLD first: touch your chin with the side of a closed fist, then pull the fist straight down toward your chest.
Immediately shape your dominant hand into an A, with the thumb resting on top of the fist.
Hold the A hand in front of you with its palm side facing left and the knuckles pointing forward.
Flick the A hand upward about three to five inches in one short, firm motion.
Keep the upward motion smaller than the -est suffix — older is a comparison, not a superlative.
tip: The -er suffix is just OLD plus the little A-hand lift; give -est the longer, bigger rise instead.

steps: Bend your dominant index and middle fingers down into a tight inverted V, like two bent legs.
Hold the V hand in the neutral space in front of you, fingertips pointing down toward the ground.
Arc the hand upward and forward in a quick leaping path, then land it back at its starting height.
Let your wrist lead the motion so the two fingers ride the arc like legs springing off the ground.
Finish with a light, springy expression — this sign is for people or primates leaping, nothing else.
tip: Save this two-legged JUMP for people and primates — a horse jumping needs the two-handed version, and a racing heartbeat needs a flutter at the chest.

steps: Point both index fingers forward into the signing space.
Start at the top-left corner of an imaginary screen at chest height.
Trace a rectangular outline with both fingertips moving together in sync.
Angle the palms slightly toward each other while tracing the rectangle.
Gaze at the traced shape with a neutral expression throughout.
Repeat with a larger outline to mean a billboard or whiteboard instead.
tip: A bigger rectangle means a bigger screen — scale the square to the object.

steps: Form a loose G hand with your dominant hand, thumb and index extended.
Bring the hand to the front of your neck near the throat.
Brush downward against your neck twice with short repeated strokes.
Aim the palm back toward your own neck as you brush.
Keep a solemn expression that suits the serious topic of clergy.
tip: Picture brushing a white clerical collar — that image is the memory aid.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing up.
Keep the flat hand steady at waist height in the signing space.
Strike its palm once with the top of your dominant X hand.
Face the striking X hand's palm back toward yourself.
Use a firm, matter-of-fact expression fitting a discussion of prices.
tip: This is the COST sign — use it for fees, fines, and prices.

steps: Bend both index fingers into hooked X handshapes.
Hold both hands at chest height, side by side.
Circle the hands around each other once, swapping sides and returning to start.
Keep the palms angled inward toward each other through the circle.
Maintain a neutral expression typical of a straightforward transaction.
tip: Picture two people trading places — that swap is the exchange.

steps: Gather your dominant fingers to the thumb, forming a flattened O.
Begin with the hand close to your chest on your dominant side.
Move the hand outward and away from your body toward the recipient.
Face the hand toward the recipient with the fingertips leading the motion.
Look at the recipient to mark who is receiving the gift.
tip: It is directional — start near yourself and end near them for 'I give you.'

steps: Shape both hands into clawed 5s, fingers spread and lightly curved.
Bring the two hands together at chest height in front of you.
Touch the fingertips of the hands together lightly, twice in a row.
Aim the palms inward toward each other as the hands meet.
Keep a neutral face, widening your eyes slightly for a bigger ball.
tip: The two claw hands outline something round — open them wider for a bigger ball.

steps: Hold your dominant 5 hand up beside your cheek.
Place the hand just in front of your face.
Circle the hand once around your face in a smooth loop.
Face the palm back toward yourself during the circle.
Raise your eyebrows slightly, as this sign often introduces a description.
tip: One circle around the face marks appearance itself, not the act of looking.

steps: Extend the index and middle fingers on both hands.
Hold the hands side by side at chest height, fingertips toward each other.
Wiggle the dominant fingers toward the other hand's fingertips in small pulses.
Angle the palms inward so the fingertips nearly meet.
Use a neutral or warm expression suited to describing a pair of people.
tip: Two finger-hands pairing up — this sign means a dating or married couple.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat and steady, fingers pressed together.
Keep it in front of your torso at waist height.
Walk your dominant fingertips along its back until they slip off the end.
Point the dominant fingertips forward as they travel and drop off.
Match your face to the outcome — sad for a bad ending, bright for a good one.
tip: The hand literally runs off the end of the track — the picture is the meaning.

steps: Curve both hands into loose C shapes with relaxed fingers.
Hold both hands out in front of your torso.
Rock the hands back and forth in a small steady rhythm.
Drive the rhythm from the shoulders and elbows, not the wrists or fingers.
Angle the palms down and toward each other, keeping space between the hands.
Keep a neutral face; the ongoing rhythm carries the activity meaning.
tip: Use this for general activity in progress, when no more specific verb fits.

steps: Raise your dominant hand with the index finger extended and the other fingers folded into a loose fist.
Hold your non-dominant hand open and flat at chest height with its palm facing upward.
Tap the side of your dominant index finger down onto the open palm of your non-dominant hand.
Repeat the tapping motion at least once more, keeping the movement quick and crisp.
Keep your dominant palm facing sideways as the index finger strikes the opposite palm.
Use a neutral, engaged expression, as if raising points in a back-and-forth debate.
tip: Think of the index finger as a gavel tapping the table — a quick double-tap signals discussion, not a single tap.

steps: Hold both hands loosely open in front of your torso, fingers relaxed and slightly apart.
Keep both palms angled toward each other as you begin pulling your hands inward.
Draw both hands back toward your chest in one smooth, welcoming motion.
Close your fingers into flat O shapes as your hands arrive at your chest, as if gathering something in.
End with your fingertips near your upper chest and your palms facing your body.
Pair the motion with an open, willing expression — you are taking the offer in.
tip: Picture pulling an offered gift against your chest — the hands closing into flat O shapes is what separates ACCEPT from merely receiving.

steps: Extend the index finger of your non-dominant hand and hold it upright at about eye level.
Extend the index finger of your dominant hand and aim it toward the tip of the base finger.
Move your dominant hand forward toward the base finger in a deliberate, aiming motion.
Stop just short of contact, hovering close to the fingertip like an arrow nearing a target.
Keep both palms angled inward so the two fingertips line up with each other.
Hold a focused, intent expression — you are locking onto a target, not touching it.
tip: Like sighting down an arrow — the base hand sits higher than usual, and the hand that never quite lands is the goal itself.

steps: Extend both index fingers and curl the remaining fingers into loose fists.
Hold both hands in front of your chest with the fingertips pointing forward.
Sweep both index fingers upward through two rolling arcs, as if drawing a cursive w in the air.
Let the wrists lead the motion, giving the arcs a smooth, buoyant roll as they climb.
Keep your palms angled downward and slightly inward while the fingertips trace the arcs.
Finish with a bright, triumphant expression — this is a celebration sign.
tip: Two upward arcs trace the w in win — reversing the roll turns the sign into FAMOUS, so keep the arcs climbing.

steps: Extend the index finger of your dominant hand, curling the rest of the fingers into a fist.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat and horizontal with the palm facing down.
Push your dominant index finger straight up between the fingers of the flat base hand.
Make the pop-up quick and sudden, as if the finger is surprising everyone by surfacing.
Keep your dominant palm facing sideways while the finger shoots upward through the base hand.
Raise your eyebrows with a slightly startled look — something has just turned up.
tip: This covers appear-as-in-show-up; for 'it appears that' use the SEEM sign instead.

steps: Curl both hands into E handshapes, folding the fingertips down to meet the thumbs.
Hold both fists up in front of your shoulders, a few inches apart.
Shake both hands frantically from side to side in short, rapid bursts.
Keep the shaking tight and urgent, like an alarm that will not stop ringing.
Turn your palms to face each other as the hands rattle back and forth.
Wear a wide-eyed, alarmed expression — your face must match the urgency of the hands.
tip: The speed sells it — a slow shake reads as a different sign, so let the E hands rattle.

steps: Pinch the thumb and index finger of each hand together to form two F handshapes.
Hold both F hands in front of your lower chest with the fingers pointing slightly down.
Drive both hands downward in one short, firm stroke, as if stamping a decision.
Stop the hands abruptly at the end of the stroke — the sudden halt carries the finality.
Keep your palms angled toward each other while the F hands drop together.
Set your jaw with a firm, resolved expression — the matter is settled.
tip: Skip the forehead touch of full DECIDE — DETERMINE uses just the sharp downward F-hand drop.

steps: Point the index finger of your dominant hand straight ahead with the palm facing down.
Raise the index finger of your non-dominant hand upright in front of your chest.
Slide the side of your dominant index finger up and down along the side of the raised finger.
Repeat the sliding motion several times with short, quick strokes, like mercury in a thermometer.
Keep your dominant palm facing down throughout, which keeps it distinct from the MONTH sign.
Hold a neutral, inquiring expression, as if asking about the reading on a gauge.
tip: Palm-down with a repeated stroke beats MONTH's palm-back single stroke — check the orientation before you sign.

steps: Curl your dominant hand into a loose fist with the thumb riding up along the side.
Press the edge of your thumbnail against the front of your chin.
Drag the thumbnail straight downward about two inches, ending near the top of your throat.
Angle your knuckles outward so the palm faces your non-dominant side during the drag.
Hold a calm, composed expression, since the sign also carries restraint and willingness to endure.
tip: Lifeprint glosses this production PATIENT, patience, restraint, and composure — the hospital-patient sense is a completely different sign.

steps: Extend the index finger of your dominant hand, folding the other fingers into a loose fist.
Touch the fingertip lightly against the center of your lips.
Snap the finger forward several inches in one quick, decisive motion.
Turn the hand so the palm faces your non-dominant side as the finger shoots forward.
Add a confident nod and steady eye contact when you are affirming that something is real.
tip: Lifeprint's actuality page directs signers to TRUE for 'existing in fact' — the same production also covers really, indeed, and absolutely.

steps: Bend the index and middle fingers of both hands downward into hooked V shapes.
Hold your non-dominant hooked hand steady in front of your chest as the base.
Sweep the dominant hooked hand downward past the base hand in one firm, deliberate stroke.
Angle both hands so the bent fingertips point downward through the whole passing motion.
Wear a strained, effortful expression that mirrors the difficulty you are describing.
tip: Lifeprint glosses this one production HARD, tough, difficult, and problem — for hard-as-in-a-rock, use the separate sign SOLID.

steps: Bring both hands up and touch your fingertips together to form a small peaked rooftop.
Hold the rooftop peak in the signing space in front of your face or upper chest.
Trace a small, quick circle in the air with the rooftop shape, like a ring of little huts.
Keep your palms angled downward and facing each other while the rooftop travels in its circle.
Use a warm storytelling expression — this storybook version suits children's tales, not everyday chat.
tip: Lifeprint says the rooftop version is functionally a myth in everyday signing — real life is a small quick CITY, a fingerspelling, or the LOCATION sign.

steps: Raise your non-dominant hand and point its index finger straight up as the base.
Shape your dominant hand into a C, with the fingers curved around the thumb.
Circle the C hand around the upright index finger without touching it.
Keep the C hand upright, palm turned sideways toward the base finger.
Use a neutral expression; this is a statement, not a question.
tip: The C handshape stands for the C in 'cultural' — this is the initialized variant of the sign for culture.

steps: Form your dominant hand into a G handshape, with thumb and index finger pinched together.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing upward, as a steady base.
Tumble the G hand forward in a full somersault movement above the base hand.
Land the pinched G hand down onto the open palm of the base hand.
Keep your expression neutral; this describes an accomplishment, not a question.
tip: The pinch of the G handshape must survive the whole somersault — opening the fingers mid-flip changes the sign.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand out flat in front of you with its palm facing down.
Raise your dominant hand and extend only the index and middle fingers together.
Rest the two extended fingers on top of the flat hand, as if sitting on it.
Tap the fingers down twice with small firm taps — this is the noun CHAIR.
Point the fingertips straight down onto the hand, keeping the palm angled downward.
Keep your face neutral; a single tap instead of two changes it to the verb SIT.
tip: The two fingers stand in for a person's legs sitting down — two taps mark the noun CHAIR, one tap the verb SIT.

steps: Form the letter B with your dominant hand, holding it at chest height.
Flick smoothly through the letters U and S in one quick blended motion.
Let the handshapes blur together instead of pausing on each separate letter.
Keep the movement compact in neutral signing space in front of your torso.
Angle your palm forward or slightly sideways for a comfortable clear read.
Maintain a neutral expression; mouthing the word lightly can help in low context.
tip: A lexicalized loan sign — fast blended B-U-S that behaves like a regular sign, not careful letter-by-letter spelling.

steps: Open both hands into loose 5 handshapes with all fingers spread wide apart.
Hold your non-dominant hand palm-up at waist height as a flat base.
Lay the back of your dominant palm-up hand onto the other open palm.
Swipe the dominant hand outward and off the base hand in one careless flick.
Keep the dominant palm facing upward through the swipe, as if tossing something away.
Wear a slightly dismissive expression — the sign carries a careless who-cares attitude.
tip: One swipe reads as squandering or wasting; it also covers WASTE-TIME when context points to squandered hours.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you, palm facing up like a page.
Form the letter D with your dominant hand, keeping the fingers rounded and upright.
Place the D hand on the flat palm and slide it forward, like flipping a page.
Repeat the slide a second time with a small crisp motion to finish the sign.
Angle the D palm slightly inward toward your body as your hand glides forward.
Keep your expression neutral and focused, like someone scanning a wordbook for a definition.
tip: An initialized sign — the letter D marks the word while the hands mime flipping pages of a paper dictionary.

steps: Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you with the palm facing up.
Shape your dominant hand into an F, pressing your thumb against your index fingertip.
Touch the F fingertips near the heel of your flat palm, then slide forward twice.
Finish with the person marker: both flat hands, palms inward, sweeping straight down past your chest.
Keep the dominant palm angled down toward the base hand during the forward slides.
Hold a matter-of-fact expression — this is a straightforward occupation label, not an action.
tip: COUNT plus the PERSON ending — Lifeprint teaches this exact form for ACCOUNTANT, and ASL dictionaries gloss the same sign for the field of accounting.

steps: Close both fists as if gripping a fishing rod, your dominant hand above the other.
Hold the rod out in front of your body at waist level.
Swing the rod up and forward in a casting motion, then repeat the cast a second time.
Keep your palms facing down toward the ground through the whole cast.
Keep your face neutral and your eyes toward the imagined line landing spot.
tip: Do a double cast for fishing — a single cast means the verb 'cast'.

steps: Curl the fingers of both hands at the middle knuckles into loose claw handshapes.
Hold your hands out in front of your chest with the fingertips nearly touching.
Interlock the clawed fingers of the two hands like gears meshing together in a machine.
Raise and lower the locked hands twice together, mimicking moving gears.
Keep the backs of your hands angled toward the sides through the motion.
Keep your expression neutral; a slight lean forward adds mechanical emphasis.
tip: The same sign covers motor, engine, and machine — context picks the meaning.

steps: Shape both hands into loose flattened O handshapes, fingertips and thumbs nearly touching.
Hold both hands up near your temples, in front of your head.
Push both hands forward about six inches in one quick motion, as if passing knowledge onward.
Open both hands into flat B handshapes with the palms facing each other.
Lower the flat hands straight down in front of your body to mark the person.
Keep a calm, respectful expression; a slight nod suits the formal title.
tip: Signs like 'teacher' — ASL has no separate honorific, so this sign covers teacher and professor.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into a flattened O, thumb pad pressed under the fingertips.
Hold your non-dominant hand low in front of you, fingers together and palm cupped upward as the base.
Move the dominant hand down and settle it into the base hand, as if placing an object where it belongs.
Keep the dominant fingertips pointing down as they land, with the base palm staying open and level.
Keep your face and shoulders neutral; this is a plain placing gesture, not an emphatic one.
tip: INSTALL is the 'put there' version of PUT — for software, keep the motion small and quick.

steps: Pinch the thumb against the index finger on each hand, forming two small pincers.
Grip your shirt fabric on each side of your upper chest, pinching between thumb and index finger.
Tug the fabric outward away from your body two or three times in short, even pulls.
Keep your palms angled down and slightly inward while you pinch and tug.
Use a neutral, describing expression — you are naming the garment, not offering to help.
tip: Use two hands for SHIRT — the one-handed version is how signers say VOLUNTEER.

steps: Shape your dominant hand into an F, thumb touching the index fingertip to close the circle.
Hold your non-dominant hand flat in front of you at chest height, palm facing straight up.
Touch the pinched tip of the F hand to the base palm near its heel, then slide it forward twice.
Keep the base palm level and facing up; turn the F hand's palm sideways during the slides.
Count with a focused, neutral face — this is a tallying motion, not a question.
tip: Add the 'person' ending to COUNT and you get ACCOUNTANT — literally 'counting person.'

steps: Bring up your dominant hand with the fingers held together and straight.
Start with the fingertips touching the center of your left breast.
Lift slightly and bring the fingertips down onto the center of your right breast in an even second touch.
Keep your palm turned toward your body so the fingertips land flat on the chest.
Keep your face matter-of-fact — BREAST is an anatomical term, not an emotional one.
tip: Two touches, left then right — the doubled movement is what makes it BREAST; it is also the base of the BREASTFEED compound.

steps: Shape both hands into bent hands with your fingers curled at the knuckles, palms facing down.
Hold your hands in front of your chest in neutral signing space.
Lay one bent hand across the top of the other hand.
Lift the lower hand over and stack it on top, moving upward with each layer.
Alternate the hands several times, each stack rising higher, as if building a brick wall.
tip: Think of stacking bricks: each hand lands on the last and the tower grows upward.

steps: Make a fist with your non-dominant hand and hold it upright in front of your chest.
Curve your dominant hand into a claw, fingers rounded as if holding a small ball.
Rest the tip of your dominant middle finger on top of the upright fist.
Circle your dominant hand around the fingertip, palm angled downward, as if the earth spins on its axis.
tip: The fist is the planet's axis; your claw hand is the earth spinning on it.
